nytimes.com.title: Pope Leo Is Recovering After Cancer Surgery, Vatican Says: What to Know
nytimes.com.text:
Pope Leo XIV had a “good” second night in the hospital after surgery to remove a cancerous nodule on his lung, the Vatican said on Thursday.
“The pope had a good night in the hospital. He got up and had breakfast,” the Vatican said on Thursday morning.
Leo’s lung cancer diagnosis has cast uncertainty over his agenda and raises questions about succession about a year and a half into his papacy.
The Vatican said that doctors operating on the pope in Rome on Tuesday confirmed he has lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer that can be highly treatable when caught early. Surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung.
It was not clear whether Leo, 71, would undergo further treatment, but the Vatican said that his recovery was proceeding as expected. The pontiff was in a “good mood,” said Matteo Bruni, the Vatican spokesman, on Wednesday.

cnn.com.title: Global tech selloff deepens as enthusiasm for AI stocks wobbles
cnn.com.text: Global technology stocks sold off sharply Thursday, as a growing list of worries, including rising borrowing costs and tougher competition from China, caused traders to sour on AI investments. Nasdaq futures were down 1.1% shortly after 6.30 a E.T. The tech-heavy index posted its worst decline since July on Wednesday, as shares of companies involved in the AI buildout, including chipmakers, tumbled. CoreWeave, a data center provider backed by Nvidia, fell 6% in premarket trading, after plunging 15.5% Wednesday. Oracle fell more than 2% premarket, having closed nearly 9% lower Wednesday. Intel, SpaceX and Nvidia were also poised to open sharply lower. “Worries about the AI buildout, bubbly valuations, lower-than-expected earnings growth at leading US frontier labs, Chinese competition, inflation and rates sent investors running for the covers,” Neil Wilson, a strategist at investment bank Saxo wrote in a note. He pointed to the slowing pace of revenue growth at Anthropic and OpenAI as adding to investor concerns. Multiple news outlets reported that Anthropic, at an investor presentation ahead of its planned IPO expected in the near future, announced its sales grew 45% to $17 billion last quarter. Growth had more than doubled in the second quarter. Further hitting sentiment, C.C. Wei, the CEO of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s largest manufacturer of advanced chips, sounded a cautious note during an earnings call Thursday. He told analysts that rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainty was challenging demand in some segments of the market. The company’s shares finished 2% lower despite bumper earnings, contributing to a 3.5% decline in an index of Taiwan’s technology stocks. South Korea’s Kospi led declines in Asia, finishing 7.6% lower on sharp drops in chipmakers SK Hynix (-11%) and Samsung Electronics (-9.5%). The scale of the decline triggered a circuit breaker, temporarily halting trading on the exchange – a frequent occurrence this year in a stock market dominated by just two stocks. Japan’s Nikkei finished 4.9% lower, with Hong Kong’s Hang Seng down 1%. An index of technology stocks in Europe fell 3% in early afternoon trade locally, with Dutch semiconductor manufacturer ASML down nearly 5%. The global retreat in technology stocks followed a sharp selloff overnight on Wall Street, after a strong US inflation print bolstered worries that rising interest rates will make it more expensive for companies to fund AI investments. Many AI companies are already heavily indebted. “A slowdown in the AI infrastructure build out would imply a sharp slowdown in US growth expectations,” Mohit Kumar, chief European economist at Jefferies said in a note. The US is spending more on AI annually as a percentage of GDP than it did on building railways across the country in the 1800s, he noted. AI stock valuations have been volatile throughout the year. The biggest hyperscalers – Anthropic and OpenAI – remain privately traded, so investors look for clues about AI demand elsewhere. One report that hints about slumping demand or higher-than-expected costs of building out AI infrastructure has frequently sent stocks on a rollercoaster ride. But fears of a bubble suddenly popping have tended to be overblown. “We expect the earnings season to justify that earnings and demand remain robust,” Kumar added. He cautioned, however, that Jefferies “would look to take some chips off the table” ahead of the midterms because a potential Democrat win in Congress “would be considered negative for the sector.” Adding to market jitters is growing competitive pressure from China, after Chinese semiconductor CXMT announced progress on advanced memory chips, raising doubts about the potential profitability of companies in the US and South Korea.

cnn.com.title: An industry is prescribing weight-loss drugs to people with anorexia, devastating lives
cnn.com.text: For AJ Jasper, drugs hailed as miracles have proven nothing short of a curse. In 2024, a hard-won truce between Jasper and the anorexia he had battled, on and off, since childhood collapsed, sending him spiraling to his lowest ebb yet. He was only a few pounds below his target weight, but a stressful period compelled Jasper to seek out a new, revolutionary class of weight-loss medication. Jasper said he submitted a form to the telehealth site Hims & Hers, lying about his weight and asking for a GLP-1 prescription. He expected to speak to a doctor. For there to be more questions. Yet in about two days, the medication was at his door. “I thought that there would be roadblocks,” he told CNN from his apartment in Chicago. CNN spoke to several clinicians and eating disorder specialists reporting sharp rises in the numbers of patients with anorexia using GLP-1s, many of whom obtained them via telehealth platforms with remarkable ease. Millions of people worldwide are using the drugs to lose weight, but their omnipresence has made it difficult for some people who have anorexia to recover or to remain in recovery. Globally, about 3.9 million people have anorexia nervosa — a complex mental health and eating disorder in which people severely restrict their energy intake to lose weight — according to the latest estimates from 2023 by the University of Washington-based Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation. A study of 436 adults with eating disorders, published in June by the University of Louisville and research institute RTI International, found that a little over 20% of those currently diagnosed with anorexia reported ever having used a GLP-1 — higher than the 15% of US adults who report using the drug at some point for weight loss. Jasper, 40, has sought treatment and stabilized and relapsed several times in the past two years. He has purchased the drugs from a number of telehealth sites, including Ro, Good Life Meds, MEDVi and Priority Meds, sometimes taking several simultaneously to maximize the effect. He’s only ever used compounded, copycat versions of name-brand drugs, as they are cheaper and come in vials rather than pre-filled pens — meaning he could administer many times the recommended dose. The nadir came in January, when Jasper’s treatment team insisted that he check into a hospital. A friend took Jasper, who, bed-bound, had become so malnourished and so underweight that he could hardly lift his head and his heart, liver and kidneys had begun to fail. “I was completely depleted,” he said. Throughout the nightmare, Jasper knew he could easily obtain what he describes as “anorexic heroin” and drop weight at a bewildering scale and speed. If one site made buying GLP-1s harder by requiring a video consultation with a clinician, he could simply use another. If a request form asked him about a history of eating disorders, he could tick “no,” and a confirmation email — arriving often within 24 hours — would inform him that the medication was already on its way. Complex rules Rules governing telehealth sites in the United States are complicated and vary state by state. All require a clinician to establish a relationship with a patient before prescribing, which can happen via a real-time video or phone call, a previous in-person meeting or through a less immediate method, like a questionnaire. Most states do not, however, allow the latter to be the sole basis of this relationship, according to the Center for Connected Health Policy. Illinois, where Jasper lives, requires, for example, optometrists to conduct in-person visits to establish a patient connection, but its rules are less explicit about how to do so for a raft of other specialties and prescription types, according to the CCHP. A spokesperson for Hims & Hers said that screening for eating disorders is a mandatory part of its prescribing process and that, as with in-person appointments, clinicians require patients to be honest about their health history. “Any answer indicating current or past disordered eating triggers additional clinical questions, closer provider review, and in many cases a referral to specialty eating disorder care off our platform,” the spokesperson said. A spokesperson for Ro said that it asks all patients to complete an intake form including questions about eating disorders. Clinicians use these details “to evaluate treatment eligibility and can, at any point, request records, require a video evaluation, or order lab testing to further understand a patient’s health,” the spokesperson said, adding that patients with a history of eating disorders are directed to “seek in-person care.” Both platforms said they regularly follow up with patients to spot problems during treatment. Jasper said he ignored any check-in emails. Telehealth platform RXPros acquired PriorityMeds earlier this year. “Patient safety and appropriate clinical oversight were central to (PriorityMeds’) processes,” a spokesperson for RXPros told CNN. MEDVi and Good Life Meds did not respond to requests for comment. Jasper has made huge leaps in recovery since January. He doesn’t want to demonize drugs that he knows are helping scores of people become healthier, nor does he want his story to be another cautionary tale. But he does want more guardrails around telehealth platforms. ‘Prescription is lax’ The Princeton Center for Eating Disorders once treated only the most severe cases of anorexia that require round-the-clock care. But the New Jersey treatment center recently introduced a program allowing patients to return home for the evening, offering more autonomy. “GLP-1 medication use has, already, in the three months this program has been open, been a major interfering factor in treatment for multiple patients,” said its director, Rebecca Boswell. She spoke of instances where patients were prescribed GLP-1s by physicians — working independently of telehealth platforms — after an in-person appointment and when an anorexia diagnosis had been well-established. Physicians uninformed about the condition have often agreed with a patient’s belief that silencing their “food noise” will help, she said. In other cases, Boswell’s patients have bought GLP-1s via telehealth sites without ever meeting a physician. Telehealth sites hit their first jackpot in the 2010s, when Viagra and other drugs for erectile dysfunction came off patent, allowing for the sale of cheaper generics. They hit another jackpot in the early 2020s, when staggering demand for GLP-1s made by pharmaceutical titans Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk led to a global shortage and regulators in the United States temporarily permitted telehealth companies to sell compounded versions. The industry as a whole has grown rapidly over the past decade and is built on the demand for drugs targeting common conditions — and that can be accessed discreetly — such as hair loss treatments and hormone replacement therapies. During the pandemic, a relaxation of some rules governing online prescribing in the US gave companies an additional boost. But the GLP-1 opportunity “kind of came out of nowhere and no one really expected it to get this big,” said Brian Tanquilut, a senior equity analyst covering the healthcare sector at investment firm Jefferies. Some company business models are based on selling high volumes of a product, he said, making a smooth pathway to prescription necessary. “Prescription is lax,” he noted of GLP-1s, which aren’t classed as “controlled substances” by the US government — those carrying a risk of addiction or abuse — and thus less strictly regulated. “Anyone who wants it can get it, for the most part.” Last year, researchers at Yale tested that impression, creating a fake profile that attempted to obtain a GLP-1 prescription through 49 different websites. The “secret shopper” study found that 92% of websites ultimately prescribed the drugs, only 55% asked about a history of eating disorders, and 33% mandated either a video or phone call with a clinician. On average, prescriptions were issued within a day. Two were issued in five minutes or less. Researchers said the results indicated that some websites were prioritizing “quick prescriptions over comprehensive care.” Regulators are just beginning to clamp down on the industry from several angles: for rampant compounding and misleading advertising in the United States, to permissive and potentially unsafe prescribing in Australia, Britain and India. Kerri Fleming, head of service development at Beat, a British eating disorder charity, said telehealth providers often ask patients to upload photos to help verify their weight. She said some sites have introduced a “live photo” system to prevent abuse. According to Fleming, some people with anorexia have falsified their image using artificial intelligence or by submitting one of a friend or family member instead. “The clinicians that work (for many telehealth sites) are very much aware of the risks and are trying to improve practices continuously,” she said. “It’s just an ever-changing landscape that is a hard one to navigate.” Kyle Zebley, chief executive officer of the American Telemedicine Association, said the risk of misprescribing is the same across virtual and face-to-face settings when patients are trusted to report on their own problems. “A questionnaire that can be gamed with false information is a clinical governance failure, not a telehealth-specific one,” Zebley said in a statement, adding that the ATA supports “rigorous enforcement against any company or clinician cutting corners on patient safety.” A spokesperson for Eli Lilly told CNN that telehealth providers prescribing its GLP-1 medications – including Mounjaro and Zepbound – operate independently and that “they use their own clinical judgement when treating patients.” Lilly “does not promote or encourage” the use of its drugs for unapproved conditions, the spokesperson said. Mette Kruse Danielsen, a communications director for Novo Nordisk, the maker of Ozempic and Wegovy, said patient safety is a “top priority” for the company and that its products are “not approved for the treatment of eating disorders.” Pervasive use Anorexia has one of highest mortality rates of any psychiatric disorder, and clinicians told CNN that frequent GLP-1 use among patients as well as the drug’s cultural ubiquity are changing approaches to treatment. They are “part of every conversation” Tom Hildebrandt is having with anorexia patients in his clinic at the Icahn School of Medicine at New York City’s Mount Sinai, many of whom report feeling encircled by family and friends taking the drugs. One patient, he said, was offered a GLP-1 at a party. Some patients seek out GLP-1s to quiet their “food noise,” Hildebrandt said. And while there is emerging evidence that the drugs could be an effective treatment for some people with binge eating disorder or bulimia, clinicians interviewed by CNN were unanimous in their rejection of any purported therapeutic benefit for anorexia. When the body is starving, the brain will return an incessant and often distressing loop of thoughts about food, an adaptive response designed to prioritize renourishment that clinicians try to harness rather than shut down. Jasper, in Chicago, understands the risk of silencing those hunger cues. He described himself as a “walking calculator” during periods of struggle with anorexia before taking GLP-1s, incessantly tracking calories ingested and expended. But he said the drugs turned him into a “zombie.” The food obsessions, fears and even nightmares went away, but so too did Jasper’s grasp of the seriousness of his condition. “(I wasn’t) even able to fully comprehend that I was actively dying. … With the medication, I was never able to realize how malnourished I was because I wasn’t thinking about food at all,” he said. He has created a petition he hopes will attract the attention of lawmakers, urging the introduction of new safeguards around online prescribing. “It’s the wild, wild West,” said Jasper.

cnn.com.title: How Trump’s megabill may be affecting you right now
cnn.com.text: When Republicans ask voters to keep them in the majority, they frequently point to the most significant policy achievement of Trump 2.0 — the tax and spending cuts bill known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Among the main selling points Republican candidates cite are popular cuts to taxes on tips and overtime, things that have a populist appeal, although many of the tax savings are more likely to benefit wealthier Americans. But the law offsets tax cut provisions by slashing federal funding for many programs that help make up the social safety net in the US, which means fewer Americans are getting aid from the government to afford food or obtain health insurance. The administration has also cited fraud, frequently without evidence, to cut down on government programs. Trump signed the law in July 2025, but some of the changes to government programs are just now coming into effect, while others won’t be felt until further down the road. Chipping away at the Affordable Care Act After failing to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act during his first term, Trump and congressional Republicans have sought to weaken it in a variety of ways. The biggest blow was their decision to let Obamacare’s enhanced premium subsidies lapse at the end of last year. The more generous assistance, which was approved in 2021 during the Biden administration as part of its response to the Covid-19 pandemic, broadened the number of people eligible for help and provided them larger subsidies. Enrollment nearly doubled between 2021 and 2025. The enhanced subsidies’ expiration, along with rising healthcare costs, sent premium payments soaring 58% for 2026. Many of those who signed up for coverage this year bought less expensive plans — though those come with higher deductibles. But many others found they simply could not afford the heftier monthly payments. As of February, enrollment fell to 19.2 million, a drop of 2.6 million from the same period a year prior, according to the latest federal data. It was the first decline in seven years. However, more people have dropped their coverage since then, according to states that run their own marketplace and CNN reporting. Some states hit harder than others Enrollment in 18 states fell 8.5% as of May compared with a year prior, according to data collected by the State Marketplace Network. It had dipped only 1.4% at the start of the year. In Mississippi, only 126,000 people were enrolled in Obamacare plans in August, a decline of 63%, the state insurance commissioner told CNN. More than 200,000 people have become uninsured. Kara Windeler, a Florida resident who has health conditions, told CNN that she must give up her Affordable Care Act coverage in November because she cannot afford the premiums. She is trying to see doctors and receive treatment before she becomes uninsured. Higher premiums mean more people will lose coverage The Trump administration has said that enrollment has fallen because many people were unknowingly signed up by unscrupulous brokers and agents and other enrollees did not exist at all. Signups are expected to drop again for 2027 since premiums are forecasted to soar for the second year in a row. Insurers have proposed a median increase of about 15% for next year, according to KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group. (Insurers’ proposed rate hikes don’t include federal subsidies, so the change in enrollees’ monthly premium payments may be different.) GOP approves the largest cuts in Medicaid history The Republicans’ “big beautiful bill” enacted the largest cuts to Medicaid since the safety net program began 66 years ago. The package is expected to slash more than $1 trillion from Medicaid and leave 7.5 million more people uninsured over a decade, according to CBO. Among the biggest changes to the program is the first-ever federal work requirement mandate. Medicaid expansion enrollees ages 19 through 64 will be required to work, volunteer, attend school or participate in a job program at least 80 hours a month, unless they are eligible for certain exemptions. Some 5.3 million more people are expected to be uninsured in 2034 because of this provision, CBO estimates. The Trump administration is also taking a harder-than-expected line on who qualifies for an exemption for the medically frail. Not only must enrollees have an illness or medical condition, such as cancer or a behavioral health issue, but that condition must also significantly impair their ability to comply with the work mandate, according to a rule issued by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services in June. The work mandate kicks in next year, but a few states opted to implement it early. In Nebraska, nearly 1,100 people lost coverage or were not able to enroll because of the work requirement since the mandate began there in May, according to state data through August. And a much higher than usual share of new applicants and those seeking to renew coverage were denied for procedural reasons, often relating to paperwork. This has led some experts to worry that people are running into hurdles that could involve the new work requirement. Millions already no longer have Medicaid coverage Overall, enrollment in Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Plan (CHIP) has declined by 5.1 million, or 6% — to 73.2 million — as of June compared with the year before, according to KFF. The number of children enrolled in Medicaid and CHIP fell by more than 2.5 million between January 2025, when Trump took office, and August, according to the Georgetown University Center for Children and Families. It’s unclear how much of the declines can be attributed to the “big beautiful bill” changes and how many children are winding up uninsured. Other provisions that are expected to strip people of coverage include a narrowing of eligibility for immigrants, such as asylees and refugees, which could also affect their US citizen children. A requirement that adults enrolled through Medicaid expansion recertify their eligibility every six months could lead some to fall off because of paperwork issues. Hospitals are sounding the alarm The “big beautiful bill” also made significant changes to the financing of Medicaid, limiting how states raise money for their share of programs and enhance payments to providers. Hospitals and other healthcare providers are concerned that these financing provisions — along with an increase in uninsured patients who have lost Medicaid and Affordable Care Act coverage — could force them to curtail services, lay off staff or even shut their doors. Some that have already had to pull back care have cited the impact of the package as one of the reasons. Trump and congressional Republicans say all these changes are meant to improve Medicaid and make sure it remains available for the most vulnerable Americans. They also argue that Medicaid should help enrollees become financially independent through work. It’s now harder for Americans to obtain food assistance The “big beautiful bill” contained several provisions that are expected to reduce enrollment in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, the formal name for food stamps, by millions of people over the next decade. The package enacted the largest cuts to food stamps in the program’s history — nearly $200 billion over a decade, according to CBO. In fact, enrollment has already fallen by more than 5 million people, or nearly 13%, between the law’s enactment in July 2025 and June, according to estimates from the left-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities that are based on US Department of Agriculture data. At least 1.5 million of them are children. While the GOP package is not the sole cause, it is a major factor, experts say. New requirement could force states to pay Among the most consequential provisions is a requirement that states start shouldering a portion of the food stamp benefit for the first time if they have a high rate of payment errors. They could be on the hook for $9 billion collectively, according to CBPP. (Historically, the federal government funded SNAP benefits, while states administered the program.) Though this measure doesn’t kick in until next October, states are being proactive in tightening their oversight and requiring more documentation from enrollees. This is leading to many people being dropped because of paperwork issues, experts say. The “big beautiful bill” also broadened SNAP’s existing work requirements to certain adult enrollees through age 64, to parents with dependent children ages 14 and older and to veterans, homeless adults and youth who aged out of foster care. Plus, the package requires states pay more of the administrative costs and ended the eligibility of refugees, asylees, victims of domestic violence and certain other immigrants. Major changes for student loans Both the “big beautiful bill” and Department of Education decisions are leading to a major overhaul of the federal student loan program. Many of the provisions kicked in on July 1, but others take effect in coming years. Federal student loans are critical to many Americans’ ability to go to college or grad school. More than 42 million borrowers have student loans, totaling more than $1.7 trillion, according to the Federal Student Aid office. The US Department of Education says the law’s reforms implement “commonsense loan limits,” simplify repayment options and improve the health of the federal student lending system. But critics worry that the program’s revamp will make it harder and more expensive for students to finance their education and to repay their loans afterwards. One of the major changes involves paying back one’s loans. The law created a new tiered standard repayment plan and a new Repayment Assistance Plan, known as RAP. These options only apply to students taking out new loans at the moment. Borrowers who are currently repaying loans won’t see any immediate changes in their options as a result of the “big beautiful bill,” but most will have to switch to one of the new plans or the Income-Based Repayment plan by July 2028. Paying for grad school could become tougher for many Graduate school students will no longer be able to borrow up to the “cost of attendance” for their programs. Instead, they will face borrowing limits that depend on what they are studying. And the Grad PLUS loan is being eliminated. In a very controversial move, the Education Department decided that certain healthcare studies — such as nursing, physician assistants and physical therapy — were not considered professional programs. That means students pursuing these careers will be more limited in their federal student loan borrowing. The decision spurred lawsuits, which are now working their way through the courts. Also, parents will be limited in how much they can borrow to help their undergraduate students. SAVE plan’s demise also affects borrowers Meanwhile, the Department of Education ended the Saving on Valuable Education (SAVE) plan — a Biden administration-era income-driven repayment plan that was blocked by federal courts in July. Borrowers are being given 90 days to switch into alternate plans, many of which may leave them with higher monthly payments. SAVE’s demise has left many borrowers worried about how they’ll afford the higher monthly payments. One speech-language pathologist in California told CNN that she and her husband are reconsidering when — or whether — they can grow their family.

cnn.com.title: Harry and Meghan make first joint appearance since returning to the UK
cnn.com.text: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have made their first joint public appearance in Britain since moving back to the country. Prince Harry and Meghan were greeted by well-wishers as they arrived at the Community Recording Studio (CRS) in Nottingham on Thursday morning. Crowds gave the couple balloons and flowers, Britain’s PA Media news agency reported, with Harry and Meghan stopping to greet onlookers and pose for selfies. Meghan told one woman in the crowd: “It’s great to be back.” The CRS is a charity that teaches film, video and music skills to young people. Inside the studio, Meghan joined a group of girls for a confidence-building and bracelet-making workshop. When asked what makes them feel most like themselves, one participant said she liked doing gymnastics, to which Meghan replied: “Our daughter is doing that too right now. She loves it,” according to PA Media. The duchess, whose Netflix lifestyle “With Love, Meghan” show centered around hosting and cooking, added: “I feel most like myself when I’m with my family and also when I’m cooking. I love doing that. I love to cook.” In a surprise announcement this summer, the couple revealed that they would be leaving their home in California to resettle in the UK, together with their two children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. The family landed in August, ahead of the start of the school year last month. They returned as private citizens and are not resuming any official duties on behalf of King Charles III. The engagement – the first of a few scheduled for Thursday – comes more than six years after the couple departed the United Kingdom for the United States and the years since have seen a public falling out with some members of the royal family. Harry and Meghan had cited tabloid intrusion, racism in British institutions, online abuse and complex family dynamics as among the reasons behind their 2020 departure. This is not the duke’s first time at CRS. He visited the studio in September last year and announced a personal donation of £1.1 million ($1.45 million) to Children in Need to assist the charity’s work tackling violence affecting young people. Harry and Meghan’s visit is not an official royal engagement. Last month, Harry’s father, King Charles, issued a letter in which he clarified that the couple should be treated as “private citizens.” The missive is said to have caught the Sussexes off guard. According to the letter, sent by the UK’s Lord Chamberlain – the most senior officer of the British royal household – all charitable work carried out by Harry and Meghan is a “personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity.” The letter also made clear that any operational issues involving them should be directed to the relevant police authorities. Harry has continued to push for the UK Home Office to reinstate his family’s taxpayer-funded security, which was downgraded when the family left for North America in 2020. The last time the Sussexes appeared together in public in Britain was four years ago, at the funeral of Harry’s grandmother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, in September 2022. While living in the US, Harry made several trips back to the UK, including for the funeral of his grandmother Queen Elizabeth II in 2022 and the coronation of his father King Charles III the following year. CNN’s Lauren Said-Moorhouse and Max Foster contributed  reporting.

cnn.com.title: Scientists find Doomsday Glacier is melting ‘more aggressively’ than thought, with big impacts for sea level rise
cnn.com.text: The planet’s widest glacier is melting “more aggressively” than previously projected, meaning its impacts on global sea level rise could be double current estimates, according to new research by a team of glaciologists. Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica — nicknamed the Doomsday Glacier because of the catastrophe its collapse would trigger — is a huge wildcard when it comes to forecasting global sea level rise. The Florida-sized glacier, which lies in one of the least accessible places on Earth, has been retreating for decades and its melting ice currently contributes around 4% to global sea level rise. But the mechanisms behind its retreat are exceptionally complex, making it tricky to precisely map out its future. It’s a vital task, however, as Thwaites holds enough water to raise sea levels by more than 2 feet if it were to collapse. Because it also acts as a cork holding back the vast Antarctic ice sheet, it could ultimately lead to around 10 feet of sea level rise, devastating coastal communities from Miami to Manila. Glaciologists from the University of California, Irvine and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory have developed a new ice sheet model they say better reflects what’s happening underneath this ice giant. Thwaites’ rapid retreat is driven by processes at its “grounding line” — the point at which the ice rises up from the seabed and starts to float on the ocean as an ice shelf. But while typical ice sheet models have tended to view the grounding line as something fixed and mostly stable, “we have come to acknowledge a different arrangement beneath Earth’s major ocean-terminating glaciers,” said the report’s lead author Mattia Poinelli, a project scientist at UCLA who was an Earth system science researcher at UC Irvine at the time of the study. Satellite data reveals the grounding line is actually a “grounding zone,” sometimes miles wide, where seawater constantly flushes in and out with the tides, lifting and lowering the thick ice in a process known as “tidal pumping.” This allows relatively warm ocean water to penetrate “deep underneath the ice sheets and causing vigorous melting,” Poinelli said. When the scientists adjusted models to include the concept of a grounding zone, they found Thwaites could contribute up to 1.2 inches of sea level rise by 2100 — twice previous estimates — even without further global warming, according to the findings published Monday in the journal Nature Communications. The land on which Thwaites sits slopes downward, meaning as the glacier melts, more ice is exposed to warm ocean water. The topography is complicated, however, by two key underwater ridges, which “pin” the ice, holding it back from flowing into the ocean more rapidly. The melting processes at Thwaites’ grounding zone are accelerating the “unpinning” of ice from a large ridge called the Mouginot Ridge, the study found. There is a 60% chance that it will be unpinned by the end of the century, the study found, after which the glacier is likely to retreat quickly down the sloping bedrock toward the next major ridge. The findings suggest the impacts of losing Thwaites might have been underestimated. A sea level rise of 1.2 inches may not sound much but it’s enough to greatly magnify dangers to coastal populations. The results “predict greater risk of and exposure for coastal flooding than anticipated in the coming decades,” said Eric Rignot, a report author and professor of Earth system science at UC Irvine. Ted Scambos, a senior research scientist for the Earth Science and Observation Center at the University of Colorado Boulder, who was not involved in the research, said the findings could be “a real gamechanger for sea level forecasting from Thwaites.” But he and other experts caution that more research is needed to understand the impacts of different grounding zone melting processes, not least by getting direct data from underneath the glacier. “The reality is that there is a lot we still need to find out about grounding zone processes to be able to make confident predictions about how fast ice will be lost,” said Robert Larter, a marine geophysicist at British Antarctic Survey, who was also not involved in the study. The environment beneath Thwaites, which is very difficult to access, is even more complex than the paper describes, he added. Getting observational data from Thwaites’ grounding line is the next step, Rignot said. The scientists are planning to travel there in 2028 to deploy instruments able to document the flushing in and out of seawater. “We have been aware of the impacts of climate change on our planet’s sensitive ice sheets for decades,” Rignot said, “but a mounting realization gained in recent years of what is really happening on the undersides of glaciers like Thwaites is leading to an even greater sense of alarm.” He said the world must cut planet-heating pollution now to limit the impacts but warned, “even if we do, we can expect higher sea levels in the future resulting from the damage that has already been done.”

cnn.com.title: Jim Jordan is quietly laying the groundwork for a run at GOP leader, sources say
cnn.com.text: When House Speaker Mike Johnson decided in September to send lawmakers home early to their districts ahead of the midterm elections, House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan quietly made clear that he would have handled the situation differently, according to a source close to Jordan. In a private conversation with one Republican lawmaker, Jordan said he would have kept lawmakers in Washington longer to hold more votes that would be politically challenging for Democrats. He also expressed interest in holding more votes on President Donald Trump’s elections overhaul bill that has been blocked in the Republican-led Senate, arguing that would help House Republicans on the campaign trail even if the bill won’t be signed into law. “Jim has a different vision on how he would have gone about this,” the source added. The episode is part of a delicate dance Jordan and his allies are engaged in behind the scenes. Publicly, Jordan says he is solely focused on helping Republicans keep the majority and supporting Johnson as speaker. But many House Republicans believe that Jordan is laying the groundwork to run for the top leadership spot if they lose the chamber, according to half a dozen lawmakers and aides. “He clearly wants to be minority leader,” a senior GOP aide told CNN. “He is fully running. He is calling candidates.” As Republicans grapple with the very real possibility they may lose the House, they are jockeying behind the scenes over who could lead their party in the minority. Johnson has also said publicly he intends to stay on as GOP leader whether Republicans win or lose the House, setting the stage for a potential clash within the party as other lawmakers eye the top spot. Asked for comment for this story, a Jordan spokesperson pointed to a previous statement in which Jordan said he was focused on winning in the midterms. A Johnson spokesperson pointed to a previous statement where Johnson said he believes Republicans will keep the majority and that he will remain their leader. Many House Republicans say the job is Johnson’s regardless of what happens in November, particularly because the speaker has Trump’s backing. Even though Jordan and Trump have a long history of working and socializing together, the president and Johnson have a strong and established relationship. But Jordan allies have made the case to some in Trump’s orbit that Jordan is in a unique position to defend Trump against Democratic investigations if Republicans are in the minority. They point to his experience leading the Judiciary committee and defending the president during both impeachments, two of the sources said. Johnson recently set off speculation about his political future after the midterms when he said in an interview with Fox News, “Heaven forbid, if we lose this majority or whatever, I don’t know what my next chapter of life is.” “If God moves on our hearts and says we should, you know, go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I’ll do that with equal fervor.” But in that same interview Johnson also projected confidence he will remain speaker. “I’m going to be the speaker in the next Congress,” Johnson said, when asked if he would run. “I’m not going to talk about the scenario where we don’t win the House, because I am laser-focused on winning the House.” Attempting to clarify his comments, Johnson said later in an interview with CBS News that his quip about starting a lawn business was meant to illustrate that his top objective, always, is to “be of my highest and best use to God and to my country.” But Johnson said if “in the unlikely scenario” Republicans lose the House majority, “I would expect my colleagues would call upon me to continue to lead the conference in divided government. My intention is to stay and serve and that’s what I’ve been doing, as best I can.” And Johnson allies point out that if he had kept the House in longer before the November midterms, Republicans would have had to take divisive votes on the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Jeffrey Epstein case files. Under Johnson, the House has voted on Trump’s elections overhaul legislation, the SAVE Act, multiple times. Jordan has yet to launch an outright campaign and his allies insist he is a team player who is not trying to undercut Johnson. But the Ohio Republican’s aggressive travel schedule ahead of the midterms to campaign for candidates running in tight races across the country, along with ramped up donations to vulnerable Republicans, has many in his party taking notice. In this election cycle through September, Jordan donated $1.97 million directly to candidates and $2.65 million to the party’s House campaign arm, according to a source familiar with the matter. Jordan has traveled to 33 states this cycle so far and this week launched a 19-day campaign swing, visiting states from Washington to Florida. Jordan ran for speaker in 2023 after McCarthy’s historic ouster, but faced opposition from moderate Republicans who didn’t know him well and felt he was too much of a conservative firebrand. Since then, Jordan has worked to mend relationships, including with those who said Jordan’s allies threatened them physically or verbally, by campaigning in their districts and donating to their campaigns. “I think he is trying to position himself for something,” GOP Rep. Carlos Gimenez, who voted against Jordan for speaker back in 2023 and backs Johnson now, told CNN. “It’s subtle. And maybe not so subtle.” Former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy is quietly making the case to some Republicans that Jordan would be a good fit to lead Republicans if they lose the majority, according to two sources familiar with the conversations. But others say Jordan is not proactively pursing any type of personal agenda. And Jordan is keeping his cards close to the vest. He even walks away from colleagues who ask him about his future, according to some sources who have tried to ask. “Having gotten to know Jim, and seeing him travel the country to help defend our majority’s swing district members, I am confident he’d rather be a rank-and-file member of the majority than have a position in minority leadership,” one GOP lawmaker told CNN. ‘A different Jim Jordan’ When members of the far-right House Freedom Caucus were summoned to the White House by Trump to discuss an expiring spy powers program in April, many looked to Jordan to represent their opposition. Jordan, the only founding member of the group still in Congress, had built his reputation on standing up to leadership, and he had voted against reauthorization of the program in 2024. But now as a chairman, he deferred to Johnson and the White House, according to a GOP lawmaker in the room. “It’s kind of a different Jim Jordan. The savagery you saw before, I haven’t seen that as much here as of late,” the GOP lawmaker told CNN. Since his failed leadership bid in 2023, Jordan has avoided the floor antics and consistent fights with leadership that Freedom Caucus members are regularly engaged in. Instead of leaning into the Republican-led investigation into Jeffrey Epstein, Jordan has barely talked about it and let House Oversight Chair James Comer be the GOP face of the work. When the panel held the high-profile depositions of Bill and Hillary Clinton in February, Jordan was instead campaigning with Republicans in the swing state of Pennsylvania. That team player and deferential mentality has become a key part of Jordan’s appeal to some reading the tea leaves about his future. He has  bought a lot of goodwill, particularly from moderates who were encouraged to see that he did not walk away after they rejected him three years ago. Instead, he took them to dinners, cut them campaign checks, and drove turnout at rallies in their districts to try to bring out base voters. “He’s taken time to build these relationships and get to know these people,” a senior GOP operative told CNN. “Helping the team out also has the added benefit of, you know, positioning.” The dynamics in the House Republican conference are also different from the last time Jordan mounted a bid. A number of lawmakers who voted against him are no longer serving in Congress. His trying to serve as minority leader with Trump as president, too, is a very different scenario than in 2023, when former Democratic President Joe Biden was in the White House and the speaker had to operate in a split government. If Democrats do reclaim the majority, Jordan’s background as a Trump-aligned attack dog and aggressive questioner of witnesses could make him a critical GOP figure, as Democrats target Trump and his administration with a deluge of investigations. Republican leadership heavily relied on Jordan to shape the party’s messaging strategy during the two impeachments of Trump, even temporarily assigning him to the House Intelligence Committee in 2019 so he could be the public face defending the president. “If you could incubate a minority leader with Trump as president and Jamie Raskin as Judiciary Chair, I don’t know how the person that comes out isn’t Jim Jordan,” a Republican close to leadership told CNN. When Jordan was campaigning with GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans in her battleground district in Virginia in September, he provided a window into how he would play defense for Trump against Democrats. (Kiggans voted against Jordan for speaker back in 2023 and said at the time that “threats and intimidation tactics” would not work on her). “It’s unbelievable what he’s been through,” Jordan said about Trump on September 26, detailing the two impeachments and various criminal investigations against him. Recounting his phone call with Trump the day the FBI searched his home in Mar-a-Lago, Jordan told voters, “When he answers, he doesn’t even say hello. He just goes, ‘Jim this is the best thing that’s ever happened to our party.’ He goes, ‘my numbers are going to go up.’” The packed room laughed. But not everyone is buying Jordan’s efforts to present himself as less of a firebrand. “I don’t think that has translated to any actual policy compromises,” one GOP source told CNN. “I think Jordan has moderated publicly and at the member level, but the staff is the same. The policy is the same.” Most Republicans argue that Johnson is their leader. But even some of Johnson’s supporters say Jordan brings some important qualities to the table. “Jim Jordan brings a lot of experience, a lot of wisdom, if you will, to Congress and to the conservative side of the aisle that we need people like Jim Jordan to be in continuing leadership roles at whatever level that might be decided by the conference after the election,” GOP Rep. Jack Bergman told CNN. “I tell you what, I don’t rule out anything because the point is, if you’re asking me who I’m supporting right now, I’m supporting Mike Johnson.” Back in February, Jordan was campaigning with GOP Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in Pennsylvania instead of questioning Clinton in Chappaqua, New York, as part of the Epstein investigation. Mackenzie, a freshman in Congress who was not yet elected when Jordan launched his speakership bid back in 2023, said he has gotten to know a different side of the Ohio Republican. The two men have bonded over family (Mackenzie’s young children and Jordan’s grandchildren are around the same age). And Jordan helped Mackenzie usher legislation through the House Judiciary Committee to expand the E-Verify program, a federal system used by employers to confirm a new hire is legally authorized to work in the US. “I think he is very well respected in our conference. And one of the things that I’ve seen and heard not just with him but other members that go through a leadership race and don’t get the outcome they are looking for, those that continue to stay in the fight and be great members of the conference actually engender and earn even more respect and support. And I think that’s what he’s done in this case,” Mackenzie told CNN in March, reflecting on his campaign visit with Jordan. Yet, planning for a reality where Republicans won’t be in the minority is a bridge most are still unwilling to cross. “We won’t be,” GOP Rep. August Pfluger told CNN when asked who he would support if Republicans are in the minority.

cnn.com.title: More than 3 million Medicare Advantage enrollees need to find new plans for 2027 in third year of turmoil
cnn.com.text: Fewer health insurance plans. Higher out-of-pocket costs. Skimpier supplemental benefits. This upheaval is what senior citizens will have to contend with when Medicare Advantage open enrollment for 2027 coverage begins on Thursday. That’s why it’s even more important that enrollees review their plan options so they aren’t hit with unexpected bills and other surprises next year, experts say. Medicare Advantage, which covers just over half of Medicare’s roughly 71 million enrollees, is going through its third year of turmoil as health insurers overhaul their offerings. The changes are largely being spurred by medical costs outpacing reimbursements from the federal government, which pays insurers to provide coverage to Medicare enrollees – though critics say that insurers are overbilling for patient care. Millions of senior citizens and other enrollees will have to find new Medicare Advantage plans because their policies are being terminated, while others could have to pay more for their coverage and care. The disruption also comes as Americans prepare to vote in the midterm elections, where the rising cost of healthcare and other necessities is a key concern. Senior citizens are a reliable voting bloc that both parties are trying to woo. President Donald Trump announced this month that he is sending a $90 payment to about 20 million senior citizens to help them cover part of their Medicare premiums – but those enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans aren’t eligible. Medicare Advantage plans had grown rapidly in popularity as insurers expanded their offerings and benefits to lure the growing senior population. They are often more attractive than traditional Medicare to budget-conscious older Americans because they have limits on out-of-pocket spending and provide some supplemental benefits, such as dental, vision and hearing coverage. However, they typically have more limited doctor networks than traditional Medicare, and certain treatments can be subject to prior authorization. But in recent years, insurers have been discontinuing their less profitable Medicare Advantage plans and seeking to stabilize their offerings, even if it means fewer policyholders. Insurers estimate that enrollment will drop to 34 million people, or 47.4% of total Medicare enrollment in 2027, though the Centers for Medicare and Medicare Services expects actual enrollment to be higher than projections and is stressing stability in the Medicare Advantage market. Open enrollment ends on December 7. “CMS is fighting to keep high-quality care options affordable and accessible for the millions of beneficiaries who rely on Medicare Advantage and Part D prescription drug plans,” CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said in a statement. Terminating coverage Nearly 3.2 million Medicare Advantage enrollees, or almost 11%, will have to shop for new policies for 2027 because their insurers are no longer offering their plans, said Jared Strock, founder of Medicare Market Insights, a weekly newsletter for the Medicare industry leaders. That compares with about 2.9 million and 2 million enrollees whose plans were terminated for this year and for 2025, respectively. Prior to that, only 1% to 2% of enrollees typically lost their plans year to year. Major insurers, including Humana, UnitedHealthcare, CVS’ Aetna and several Blue Cross and Blue Shield carriers, are among those culling their offerings or pulling out of geographic areas, according to Strock, who reviewed CMS data. Many of the plans being canceled are preferred provider organization, or PPO, policies, which give patients more flexibility and include out-of-network coverage. To be sure, most enrollees will still have a choice of multiple policies. The average beneficiary will have 28 Medicare Advantage plans with prescription drug coverage to select from, although that’s down from a high of 36 plans in 2024, according to KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group. Still, a small but growing share of older Americans will not have any of these plans in their area. Some 638,000 people in 193 counties will be in this situation for 2027, up from 399,000 people in 123 counties this year, according to KFF. The number of plans offered varies widely by state and county, said Haitham Aly, a principal at Oliver Wyman, a consulting firm. Rural residents are more likely to see insurers pull out, but those living in the Southeast typically have a wider array of choices. “It’s very regionally driven,” he said. “There are some states where there’s minimal disruption as far as plan offerings to consumers. There are other states where there are a lot more drastic changes happening.” Overall, there will be 5,532 Medicare Advantage plans next year, decreasing by only 21, according to CMS. But that figure includes so-called special needs plans that cater to specific categories of enrollees. Insurers are expanding their selection of policies for those with chronic conditions – particularly certain heart and lung diseases and diabetes. One incentive to do so is that they receive higher federal reimbursements for sicker enrollees. Some 744 chronic condition plans are available for next year, up from 376 in 2025, according to Strock. Enrollment in those types of plans has skyrocketed to more than 1.8 million, up from about 401,000 in the fall of 2021. Insurers are also expected to trim the generosity of their supplemental benefits, though CMS has yet to release its overview of these offerings for 2027, experts said. Enrollees may find that their dental and hearing benefits don’t cover as much care as they have in the past, their medical transportation benefits are curtailed or their allowances for over-the-counter products are reduced. Uptick in costs Many enrollees whose plans are not being terminated could see their costs increase for 2027, which is why they need to review their options. Insurers are trying to return to or boost the profitability of their policies as they contend with higher prices and greater healthcare usage among patients. Average monthly premiums, weighted for enrollment, will dip 7% to $12.11 overall, but much will depend on what type of Medicare Advantage policy an enrollee has, Strock said. The plans that don’t cater to people with chronic conditions or other special needs will see their premiums jump 23% to $14.80 a month. Just over 1 in 5 people with non-special needs coverage will be hit with a premium increase. The plans for those with chronic conditions, on the other hand, will be less expensive. Meanwhile, insurers are also raising the out-of-pocket limits that enrollees will face, leaving them on the hook for more of the cost of care. On average, the enrollment-weighted maximum for in-network services will be $6,603, up 9% from this year, Strock said. Some 70% of enrollees will see their out-of-pocket cap increase, compared with 35% for this year. And nearly three-quarters of enrollees will have to pay more for prescription medications, with the average enrollment-weighted deductible jumping 23% to $509 for plans with drug coverage. Only 12% of enrollees are expected to be in plans with no deductible, down from 60% in 2024. “Better funding brought Medicare Advantage premiums down for 2027, but a record number of seniors will have to find new coverage, and many will pay more when they need care,” Mary Beth Donahue, CEO of the Better Medicare Alliance, a coalition of insurers, providers, business groups and community organizations that advocates for Medicare Advantage, said in a statement to CNN. “Seniors shouldn’t have to face this disruption every year.” Standalone drug coverage Those in traditional Medicare who buy standalone Part D drug policies from insurers will also see some changes for 2027. More than 1 million people are losing their Part D plans and will have to pick new options, said Brooks Conway, principal at Oliver Wyman. CVS’ Aetna is leaving the market, which is dominated by Humana and Centene. No plans with $0 premiums will be available, though almost every state will have policies with monthly premiums of less than $20, he said. Part of the reason is that Trump discontinued a Biden-era subsidy for insurers aimed at stabilizing their costs after the Democrats’ Inflation Reduction Act in 2022 left carriers on the hook for more of the drug spending by sicker enrollees. While CMS is highlighting that the average Part D monthly premium will increase less than $1 to $36 for next year, some insurers are hiking premiums by more than $50 a month. So enrollees should check the cost of their plans for 2027. “Those people won’t be technically forced to shop, but if they do shop, they’ll have significant premium reductions,” Conway said.

cnn.com.title: How a celebrity cat inspired the construction of the world’s largest wildlife corridor
cnn.com.text: In a city best known for its movie stars, one of Los Angeles’ most beloved residents always stood out among the rest: he strutted through the streets in a tawny-colored coat, walked on all four paws and had a habit of wandering alone at night. The California mountain lion, known as “P-22,” journeyed across two of the busiest freeways in the United States to take up residence inside Griffith Park — one of Los Angeles’ most popular urban parks. Using remote camera traps, wildlife photojournalist Steve Winter captured an iconic image of P-22 roaming beneath the illuminated Hollywood sign at night in 2013. The photo helped catapult the cougar to international stardom. “People fell in love with this cat, he was a celebrity in the land of celebrities,” Winter said. “It was like a movie.” Seen resting in backyards and grazing on garden plants, P-22 amassed a huge following as he was caught on more of Winter’s camera traps and residents’ security cameras around the park’s neighborhoods. But his small 6.7-square-mile range inside Griffith — and his ventures into densely urban spaces — ultimately led to his decline. Due to severe injuries caused by a car collision, combined with illness, he was euthanized in 2022. The famous feline’s story highlights a much bigger problem facing all big cats: they are losing land — and some have lost more than 90% of their former range. “It’s not only that animals are losing habitat, but remaining habitat is becoming really fragmented, with areas often cut by roads that are nearly impossible to cross,” environmental journalist Sharon Guynup told CNN. “They’re prisoners in these areas,” Winter said, “so we need to find a way to give animals the opportunity to cross these roads that have them hemmed in.” The plight of P-22 helped bolster a movement to create the world’s largest wildlife overpass across greater Los Angeles’ 10-lane Highway 101 — the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing. It connects the Santa Monica Mountains and the Sierra Madre Range, two significant stretches of wild territory in the region. The 165-foot-wide crossing is set to open December 2, allowing wildlife to flow freely above the traffic below. Winter and Guynup have spent decades documenting big cat species all over the globe. Winter with images and Guynup with words, the two combine strong visual and written storytelling in their new National Geographic book, “Big Cats.” “We didn’t want to make this a greatest hits photo book; we wanted to focus on stories that had tangible impact,” Guynup said. From exposing illegal wildlife trade to inspiring conservation legislation, their book takes readers behind the lens of some of their most risky but rewarding work to help save big cat populations around the world. And for Guynup, the stakes extend far beyond the animals themselves: “We need the entire spectrum of life to keep ecosystems healthy, and big cats have an outsized role in that process,” she said. Changing perspectives on Brazil’s jaguars The Brazilian Pantanal, the world’s largest tropical wetland, is home to one of the biggest concentrations of jaguars on Earth. It was here, while coasting through the waters of Corixo Negro in 1997, that Winter encountered his first jaguar while on assignment for National Geographic’s first major feature story on the big cats. At the time, Winter said, local ranchers believed that the jaguars were killing their cows, “so they thought the only good jaguar was a dead jaguar,” he told CNN. They were hunted in retaliation, their fur sold for profit. Winter began working with biologist Sandra Cavalcanti, who through GPS collar tracking, was able to prove that cattle make up less than a third of the jaguars’ diet, which can include up to 85 different animals. Other factors, such as disease and malnutrition, caused more cattle deaths than jaguars. Cavalcanti’s research, alongside Winter’s photographs in National Geographic, helped change the narrative around jaguars — from something feared, to something worth protecting. By identifying the Pantanal region as a hotbed for wild jaguar sightings, Brazil saw economic value in keeping these animals alive and investing in wildlife ecotourism. “Now, Jaguars are worth more alive than dead and numbers have increased despite droughts and increasing wildfires, and people are much less likely to kill them now because they bring a lot of money into the area,” Guynup said. Exposing an illegal tiger trade in Thailand In 2011, Winter was covering a story on two subspecies of tigers thought to be the next to go extinct — one being the critically endangered Indochinese tiger, found exclusively in Thailand and Myanmar. Winter visited Thailand’s Tiger Temple, a Buddhist monastery and popular tourist attraction where people paid to pet and pose with Indochinese tigers. Wat Pha Luang Ta Bua temple billed itself as an animal sanctuary, but for years, conservationists suspected its involvement in the black-market trade of tigers and their body parts. After Guynup and Winter published a book featuring photos from the temple, Guynup was contacted by wildlife biologist Sybelle Foxcroft, who said she could help prove that the temple was involved in an illegal wildlife trafficking ring, Guynup recounted. Guynup and Foxcroft spent a year working inside sources, obtaining CCTV and audio recordings, and uncovering documents proving the temple was tied to the illegal trade. “When the story ran in 2016 it kicked up a furor both domestically and internationally, and within four months, the [Thai] government went in and confiscated the tigers and shut it down,” Guynup said. Taking down the “Tiger Kings” in the US A few months before the popular Netflix documentary series “Tiger King” first aired, Guynup and Winter released a 30-page feature in the December 2019 issue of National Geographic, exposing the scale of big cat breeding and exploitation in the US. “We had more tigers in captivity in the United States than were left in the wild in Asia,” Guynup said. Together, they documented a vast network of big cat attractions across 32 states — from small roadside zoos to large circus shows, many offering cub-petting and photo opportunities to the public for a steep price. Guynup even interviewed the infamous Doc Antle, then known as one of the biggest tiger breeders in the US, featured in Tiger King. Through Winter and Guynup’s multi-year investigation, they uncovered the industry’s abuse of these big cats alongside the illegal trafficking of the animals. Their investigation helped lay the groundwork to pass the Big Cat Public Safety Act in 2022, which bans private ownership, breeding or sale of big cats, except for accredited institutions. When the story came out, a copy was given to every member of Congress, Guynup recalled. “Look, bills are boring to read, but if you’re looking at photographs and reading a narrative, then I think it can engage hearts and minds in a really positive way,” Guynup said. Ultimately, protecting big cats means safeguarding entire ecosystems. “When you protect a top predator, or a wide-ranging species, you protect a large area,” Guynup added, “and that protects everything that shares land with that species.”

cnn.com.title: Pakistan school roof collapse kills at least 32 children and one teacher
cnn.com.text: Thirty-two children and a teacher were killed and dozens injured when the roof of a school in northern Pakistan collapsed on Thursday morning, authorities said. Heavy overnight rainfall caused the roof of a two-story building at Al Khair Public School in the city of Peshawar to become unstable and later collapse, Bilal Ahmed of the local rescue services told CNN. The deceased children ranged in age from six to 14 years old, according to Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar, where the victims were taken. A 25-year-old woman is also listed among the fatalities. Some children are still trapped in the rubble and rescuers are working to reach them, Ahmed said. Around 50 children were injured in the collapse, according to hospital figures. Several remain under medical observation. Video from the scene obtained by CNN showed ambulances rushing through narrow streets and crowds gathered outside the school building. Local residents were among the first people to reach the scene, and rescue workers arrived within minutes, eyewitnesses said. Building collapses are a common problem in Pakistan. Construction standards in the country are often poorly enforced, and many structures are built with substandard materials. Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari said the incident was a “heart-wrenching tragedy” and called for a comprehensive investigation into the cause of the deadly collapse. “In this hour of sorrow, the entire nation shares equally in the grief of the affected families,” the president’s office posted on X. The school’s owner has been arrested, and an investigation launched into the incident, a police official in Peshawar, Muhammad Ali, told CNN. The collapse comes just weeks after a fire tore through a hospital in the capital Islamabad, killing at least 14 newborns and sparking widespread anger and multiple arrests. The fire was confined to a third-floor nursery but officials said it spread so quickly that staff were able to rescue only one baby from among the 15 being cared for there. An inquiry found that the nursery had no fire alarm or sprinkler system and that the hospital lacked detailed procedures and training for responding to fires and other emergencies. In July, a roof collapse at a tutoring center under construction in Pakistan’s eastern city of Lahore killed at least 14 schoolchildren, police and rescue officials said at the time. This is a developing story and will be updated.

cnn.com.title: New North Korea-China bridge finally opens. But will it help Pyongyang evade sanctions?
cnn.com.text: Ultra-isolated North Korea has a new bridge to the outside world. It’s a four-lane highway leading to close ally and main trade partner China, and its opening on Thursday marks the latest rapprochement with Beijing. Experts worry it may also make it easier for Pyongyang to evade sanctions over its illegal nuclear program. The nearly two-mile New Yalu River Bridge links the Chinese border city of Dandong with North Korea’s Sinuiju. Construction was completed in 2014, but the bridge remained unused for years because connecting roads and border facilities on the North Korean side were unfinished. Satellite imagery from earlier this month showed vehicles on the bridge connecting Dandong and Sinuiju, which are believed to account for about 70% of bilateral trade, and on Thursday an opening ceremony saw trucks decked out with national flags making the journey over the river. The older Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, also located in Dandong and built in 1937, has traditionally served as the main crossing between the two countries. But with just one lane, it can accommodate traffic in only one direction at a time. The long-delayed opening follows a period of improving relations between Beijing and Pyongyang, including the reopening of a railway connection in March and Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s visit to Pyongyang in June for a summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. That summit hinted at a restoration of ties between the two Communist states after they grew more distant in recent years as North Korea grew closer to Russia, analysts say. The bridge offers an opportunity for China and North Korea to demonstrate the restoration of their relationship and their strategic alignment to the international community, Lim Eul-chul, a professor of North Korean studies at Kyungnam University in South Korea told CNN. China still accounts for about 95% of North Korea’s total official trade, and the South Korean government has reported 17 rail and vehicle links connecting China and North Korea, according to the AP. Last month, North Korea inaugurated the first road bridge linking it to Russia. Ahead of the opening, a spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry said: the bridge “will further promote economic and trade exchanges and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries, and enhance the well-being of their peoples.” Some analysts worry that it will also help the world’s most-sanctioned country evade bans on exports of its raw materials and other goods. Kyungnam University’s Lim said North Korea could use the crossing as a government-controlled gateway to circumvent UN sanctions. And, to what China is willing to go along with that, is partly contingent on relations with the US, said Yang Mu-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, “As relations between Washington and Beijing have become strained, China tended to take a more passive approach to enforcing sanctions,” Yang said.

cnn.com.title: Two cargo ships sunk in Strait of Hormuz as Iran ramps up attacks in run-up to midterms
cnn.com.text: Two cargo ships have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being struck by unknown projectiles in separate incidents – highlighting the heightened danger to shipping as Iran steps up attacks in an attempt to regain control over the critical waterway. The Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pride was struck on Tuesday while passing through the strait, catching fire and later sinking, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. All crew members were safely evacuated. Videos verified by CNN show black smoke rising from the ship as it takes on water, while later footage and satellite images show cargo scattered in the water and a small oil slick. Iranian state media Press TV reported that the ship had “hit a sea mine on an unauthorized route” – which experts cast doubt on, saying a drone attack was more likely. The merchant vessel Cape Dao, registered under Antigua and Barbuda, also sank, according to data from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) on Wednesday – after it was first hit by projectile on September 23. One Indian crew member was killed. While many vessels have been hit in the Strait of Hormuz this year, these are only the second and third to have sunk in the Middle East since the Iran war began in February, according to IMO data. Attacks have ramped up significantly since the end of September, once again reducing the amount of oil transiting out of the Middle East and raising oil prices around the world. That’s been a consistent headache for US President Donald Trump as the midterm elections approach, with gas prices, tariffs, and other factors driving up the cost of living top of mind for many voters. Data from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which monitors shipping incidents, shows just how high the risk is. Nine attacks in or near the Strait of Hormuz have been reported since Monday, including a drone strike on a tanker. Only 4.147 million barrels of oil successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz on Monday – less than a quarter of pre-war levels, according to maritime data tracking service Kpler. And the seven-day average of oil flow through Hormuz has dropped sharply since early October, Kpler’s data shows. “The sinking of Singapore-flagged GFS PRIDE marks a dangerous escalation after weeks of near-daily attacks on commercial shipping. Iran claims a naval mine; but a drone strike is more likely,” said former US Navy officer Charlie Brown, also a senior adviser for United Against Nuclear Iran, a nonprofit that tracks and reports on Iranian sanctions violations. “Many ask what response will the US Navy mount to Iran’s escalating attacks on global shipping,” he added. “But the real question is what response will other nations take? How long will the world tolerate this threat to shipping, seafarers and freedom of navigation?” The US military continues to enforce a blockade on Iranian ports to maintain economic pressure on Iran. To some extent, it’s worked: Iran’s economy is in tatters, and in recent months it clearly lost its leverage over the strait, with the amount of oil flowing from other Gulf nations through the waterway increasing to near-normal levels. That’s partly thanks to a complex operation involving US-military-escorted “dark” transits across the strait at night, with tankers turning off their transponders to avoid detection. That rise in oil flow is why Iran is now ramping up its attacks and threats, hoping to wrestle back the leverage it once had over the strait – especially as American voters head to the polls. The Trump administration has tried to lower prices in other ways, including a controversial deal announced last week to drop some sanctions on Russia to import a relatively small amount of the country’s diesel. But this has been met with bipartisan criticism – and there’s no guarantee it will bring any substantial relief, with analysts warning that diesel could climb near all-time highs by November.

cnn.com.title: Exclusive: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran, sources say
cnn.com.text: The US military has developed new strike plans that include potentially using the so-called “mother of all bombs” to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites should President Donald Trump give the order to resume combat operations either before or after the midterm elections, according to multiple US officials familiar with the matter. Using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb or MOAB, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, for the first time in the conflict with Iran would mark a notable escalation, even though there are doubts over how effective it would be in accomplishing any of Trump’s stated strategic objectives or tipping the balance of the war, multiple sources familiar with internal military planning discussions about potentially deploying the weapon said. Trump is facing pressure to bring an end to the deeply unpopular war — as Republicans brace for potential political backlash from voters in the upcoming midterm elections and there is little indication the two countries are close to a negotiated resolution after more than six months of US bombing. While the US military continues to provide Trump with options for potential strikes against outstanding Iranian targets, some officials continue to privately question whether the White House has a strategy that incorporates those plans in a way that could actually end the war — something only the president has the power to do. For months, Trump and his advisers have discussed options that could act as a “definitive” end to the war, at least from a messaging point of view, aware of how unpopular the conflict has become among Americans. While some administration figures have characterized the war as essentially won, Trump has been more guarded in recent remarks, stopping short of declaring victory and saying the US still has unfinished business in the country. Behind the scenes, Trump has also cast doubt on some outside allies who have encouraged him to simply bring US troops home and move on. Doing so, Trump has argued, would look like defeat. Over the course of the last several weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various options for Iran. While Trump announced publicly that he would not take new actions before the midterms, several advisers said privately they didn’t know whether that statement was definitive or could change before Election Day. Trump has ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iranian targets that include “a lot of energy infrastructure” and the potential use of a MOAB, one of the sources told CNN. The same source said the phrasing used was that this attack would come “prior to US retrograde in CENTCOM AOR (area of responsibility),” indicating the administration could launch the additional strikes, attempt to declare victory and quickly pull everyone out. A second source told CNN that military plans for striking Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain, also explicitly call for using the MOAB. In recent months, Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Pickaxe, where the US and Israel believe Tehran has stored components of its nuclear program, even after pausing full combat operations earlier this year, and Trump continues to emphasize that his goal is to ensure Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon. Doubts MOAB would be effective Another US official noted that when the military plans, it develops a menu of options for policymakers that range from the high-end to low-end. Higher-end targets, including those that are located deep underground, require bigger bombs, and the MOAB is the biggest, the official added. But there are questions around whether the MOAB would be an effective munition to use against Iran’s nuclear facilities and other sites that are located deep underground.
