While the GPS-guided bomb is capable of destroying an area equivalent to nine city blocks, it likely lacks the capability to penetrate deep enough under the surface to destroy the suspected nuclear facilities at Pickaxe, which is believed to be fortified by layers of granite, and other remaining Iranian nuclear sites, sources said. “The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” a third source familiar with military planning discussions around Iran told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.” If used, the MOAB would have devastating effects on the area that it impacts but likely only at the surface level, the sources noted. And the bomb’s massive blast radius would almost certainly raise concerns about the prospect of civilian casualties — particularly if it is used to target Iranian infrastructure targets located near populated areas and in close proximity to non-military sites. Still, Trump could opt to use the MOAB as a psychological weapon at a time when the Iranian regime appears dug in and unwilling to bend to his diplomatic demands. While US officials warn that deploying it is unlikely to force Iran’s capitulation or achieve a strategic military victory — it could provide Trump with an additional option, short of restarting full combat operations, to alter the conflict’s current status quo. “POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level … you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped,” the third source familiar with recent planning discussions added. Many within the administration as well as outside analysts agree that the only way to decisively defeat Iran would be through a major operation involving ground troops, a commitment that could potentially cost thousands of American lives. The Pentagon considers all scenarios, so those plans exist, but as of now no one in the administration is arguing for such drastic action. Trump has indicated he has little interest in putting US boots on the ground in Iran but his desire to end the conflict as soon as possible presents a political dilemma for a president who is keenly aware of how unpopular the war has become yet has been unable to secure a diplomatic agreement that would bring it to a close. Top Trump administration officials and military planners have been focused, for weeks, on finding an off-ramp that gives Trump a “symbolic” win — at minimum — he can try to sell to the American people without preventing a potential diplomatic breakthrough, starting with an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, CNN has reported. A fourth source familiar with the Pentagon’s recent planning discussions on Iran told CNN that military officials had developed some options that would amount to a “fireworks show,” with the goal of providing Trump an off-ramp from the conflict even if those strikes fail to accomplish his stated goals for starting the war in the first place. And despite Trump’s recent pledge to hold off on launching additional strikes before the midterms, the US military already appears to be preparing for potential Iranian retaliation should the president give the go-order. The next turnover of US troops deployed to CENTCOM is also expected to take place within the next few weeks, according to a fifth source, a US official who acknowledged it is possible some of the personnel who rotate out of the region, may not be replaced by fresh service members. Asked about the plans, a White House official told CNN that they do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist, adding “President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon.” In response to CNN’s request for comment, a Pentagon official said: “The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary‑level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment.” MOAB developed for ‘psychological operations’ Developed during the Iraq War, the MOAB is an air blast-type warhead that explodes before hitting the ground to project a massive explosion from all sides. During the  final stages of testing in 2003, military officials told CNN the MOAB was mainly conceived as a weapon employed for “psychological operations.” Military officials said then they hoped such a huge blast would rattle Iraqi troops and pressure them into surrendering or not even fighting. As originally conceived, the MOAB was to be used against large formations of troops and equipment or hardened above-ground bunkers. The target set has been expanded to include targets buried under softer surfaces, such as caves or tunnels. Trump was the first US president to deploy the MOAB, during his first term when he authorized the military to use its most powerful non-nuclear bomb on ISIS positions in Afghanistan in 2017. That strike targeted a network of fortified underground tunnels that ISIS had been using to stage attacks on government forces — killing 36 ISIS fighters, Afghan officials said. The blast destroyed three underground tunnels as well as weapons and ammunition, but no civilians were hurt, Afghan and US officials added at the time. At the time, the bombing marked a dramatic change in attitude for Trump, who advocated an isolationist, “America first” foreign policy during his first election campaign. Following the 2017 strike, US military officials were pressed on whether the 21,600-pound bomb was necessary for that particular target and would likely face similar questions if the munition is deployed against Iran.

cnn.com.title: Suspicious letters with white powder sent to election offices in multiple states
cnn.com.text: Election offices in multiple states reported receiving suspicious letters in the mail this week containing a powdery white substance, prompting an investigation from the FBI and US Postal Inspection Service. Officials in Louisiana and Oklahoma confirmed receipt of such letters on Tuesday and said they evacuated their election offices while law enforcement responded to the incidents. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said Wednesday his office was the “intended recipient” of a suspicious letter but that the Postal Service intercepted it. No one was reported harmed in any of the incidents. In a statement Wednesday night, the FBI said “a series of suspicious mailings” have been sent to “various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.” “Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the FBI said. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.” The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said they were “deeply concerned” by the incidents. “As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy,” said a joint statement from the two organizations. “Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties.” Election officials across the country are no strangers to suspicious or threatening mail. Powder-containing packages were sent to election officials in at least six states just weeks before the 2024 presidential election. The incidents reported this week show that “in the current threat environment, election and law enforcement officials must be prepared to address a broad range of cyber and physical threats,” John Cohen, a former acting undersecretary for intelligence and analysis at the Department of Homeland Security, told CNN. “The bad news [is that] the threat is rapidly evolving, dynamic, technologically enabled and dangerous,” Cohen said. “The good news [is that] state and local officials are better prepared than ever to address these threats.”

cnn.com.title: Talarico tackles abortion, faith and ‘conspiracy theories’: Takeaways from the CNN & Jubilee town hall
cnn.com.text: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico appealed face-to-face to skeptical Republicans and independents Wednesday night in a joint town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee, framing the election in populist terms and insisting he is willing to break with his own party if doing so benefits the state. “I’m a proud Texas Democrat, but I already have a religion and I already have a sports team,” he said. “So, I have no problem sharing hard truths with my party if it’s what’s best for Texas.” Talarico faces Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in one of the most important Senate races of November’s midterm elections. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to claim the Senate majority, and flipping a GOP-held seat in Texas would be a significant boost to that effort. Talarico, a former seminary student, peppered his remarks with references to his “spiritual heroes” and made references to the last three popes. He said he felt he could find common ground with conservatives — in part by looking to solutions to the problems that fuel cultural divides, rather than treating those divides as a political hammer with which to “beat each other over the head.” And as he campaigns for the votes of independents and moderate Republicans in Texas, where Democrats haven’t won statewide in three decades, he attempted to frame the election in populist terms — regular Americans against wealthy individuals and corporations. “The only minority destroying America is the billionaires,” Talarico said. Paxton — who has refused to debate Talarico and has not responded to an invitation to hold his own town hall — was absent from nearly all of Wednesday night’s discussions. Talarico only circled back to the topic of his Republican opponent at the end, after telling the audience that he doesn’t “want people to vote just against Ken Paxton. I want them to vote for me.” But he took one big swing at Paxton in the final minutes. “We have an opportunity in this race not just to defeat the most corrupt politician in Texas; we have an opportunity to defeat this entire corrupt system,” he said. Here are takeaways from Talarico’s town hall: Courting a broad spectrum of voters Talarico repeatedly sought to reach out to the Republican and independent voters he’ll need to win in deep-red Texas, emphasizing that there is common ground to be found — an effort that was on display when he was challenged by a woman who opposes abortion rights. Talarico told the woman that “it’s OK that you and I come to different conclusions” about the moral and theological questions surrounding the issue. “What I think we can do is actually come together on reducing the number of unplanned pregnancies and the number of abortions,” he said. “Because if we treat this issue as a public health problem and not a culture war problem, then we can actually make progress together.” It was one of several ways Talarico looked to make appeals across the aisle on Wednesday night. He also emphasized his willingness to break with the Democratic Party. He called the national debt “an emergency” and said policymakers should seek to run the federal government more efficiently. He broke with progressives’ calls for aggressive breaks from fossil fuels to combat climate change, emphasizing his support for Texas’ oil and gas industry and declaring that he endorses an “all of the above energy strategy.” He also declared himself “a border security Democrat” and criticized former President Joe Biden’s administration’s management of the US-Mexico border. Asked if he supports abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement — a position held by many progressives within his party — Talarico quickly responded: “No, and I never have.” He then argued that President Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts have gone too far, and that the president has deployed ICE as a “secret police force.” “We don’t want federal agents murdering our neighbors before our very eyes,” he said. ‘Nasty case of the flu’ Talarico opened the town hall by addressing his recent absence from the campaign trail that lasted more than a week and fueled Republican attacks that at times veered into debunked conspiracy theories. Talarico returned to making public appearances on Friday. Talarico reiterated that he had a “nasty case of the flu” and said he now feels “much better.” Looking back, he said he would not have handled the absence differently, “I think the responsible thing to do when you have something like the flu is stay at home and not get other people sick,” Talarico said, adding that he was able to work remotely. Talarico knocked Paxton and the “conspiracy theorists” for their attacks over his absence, calling them a distraction from issues that are more important to voters. “Conspiracy theories don’t put food on the table,” Talarico said. Clarifying past statements Talarico sought to clarify a number of comments he has made in recent years that have drawn scrutiny as he runs for Senate. One of those comments came in 2020 during a Sierra Club event where he called capitalism an “oppressive system.” Talarico took issue with the media’s characterization of the remark and said he was referring to a “crony capitalism” that disproportionately benefits the wealthy. “What I’m trying to get back to is OG capitalism where we actually reward work instead of wealth,” Talarico said. Talarico was also asked about a Senate primary debate in January where he criticized Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He said at the debate that it was “time to tear down this secret police force and replace it with an agency that actually is going to focus on public safety.” Talarico said he does not support abolishing the agency. “We need Immigration and Customs Enforcement in this country, but that’s not what we’re seeing,” Talarico said. “What we’ve seen over the last year is a secret police force, and that’s what we don’t want in this country.” Later, Talarico was confronted again about his 2021 comment that “God is non-binary.” He reiterated that he was “being provocative” when he said it. Connecting health scare to economic message Talarico has framed his entire campaign around his willingness to take on big business and wealthy interests — and used the emotional story of his own diabetes diagnosis as he laid out one example of how he said he wants to do so. The 37-year-old Talarico choked up briefly as he explained that in 2018, during his first campaign for the state legislature, he walked 25 miles across his district in one day — and then fell ill and slept for 36 hours. He was hospitalized and diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. Talarico said when he went to Walgreens to pick up his prescribed insulin for the first time, he learned the cost was $684 — money he did not have at the time. That was the impetus behind his successful push to cap insulin copays in Texas at $25 per prescription, he said. If he is elected to the Senate, Talarico said he would push to similarly cap costs across the nation for other medical necessities, including cancer drugs and EpiPens. He also said he would seek to roll back cuts in Affordable Care Act spending imposed by congressional Republicans and Trump in 2025, and would push for a new “public option” that would allow Americans to purchase health insurance coverage from a government-run program. “These for-profit corporations are making billions of dollars in profit off our pain,” Talarico said. “If you’re willing to take on this corrupt system, then you can actually make change for people.” Facing scrutiny of his Biblical interpretations At least two voters challenged Talarico on his liberal interpretations of the Bible — and the candidate sought to find common ground with them. One of those voters was a Catholic Texan who described herself as a “one-issue” voter on abortion. Talarico told her that some of his “spiritual heroes,” such as Pope Leo, are “pro-life” and that he “can respect anyone like you who is consistently pro-life.” “We’re both Christians, and the Bible is silent on the issue of abortion,” Talarico said. “It means you and I both have to look at different scriptures to try to come to a conclusion. But what I think we can do is actually come together on reducing the number of unplanned pregnancies and the number of abortions.” The voter disputed Talarico’s claim that the Bible does not address abortion, pointing to the Ten Commandments, one of which says, “Thou shalt not kill.” Talarico responded sympathetically, saying it was “OK that you and I come to different conclusions about that.” Another voter, a Republican named Sarah Gardner, also raised issues with how Talarico has used his faith to argue the Democratic position on social issues. She said people “need to be careful using modern cultural terms when talking about God.” Talarico agreed, saying it was a “very fair criticism.” This article has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: OpenAI accuses former employee of leaking intel on AI device to Apple
cnn.com.text: OpenAI is accusing a former employee of stealing intellectual property related to an unreleased device and later sharing some of the information with Apple. The employee, OpenAI alleges, had previously worked at Apple, then joined OpenAI for six months, before going back to Apple, according to a court filing from OpenAI on Wednesday. The company said the employee downloaded over 100 highly confidential files to his personal accounts before rejoining Apple. The transferred files include “detailed images of the unreleased device(s), as well as highly confidential engineering and manufacturing data about the device(s),” according to the filing. The last file was sent in June on the employee’s final day, OpenAI alleges. OpenAI went on to claim the former employee, who it did not name, “made a presentation about OpenAI’s product plans to Apple’s senior leadership, including Apple’s vice president of operations in Asia.” “That presentation appears to have happened months ago—and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products,” OpenAI wrote in the filing. Apple told CNN it has found no evidence to support the allegations and that it has strict policies in place to make sure new employees don’t use confidential information from previous workplaces. The company also said it would work with OpenAI to remediate any of OpenAI’s information found on Apple’s systems. Apple accused OpenAI of trying to create a distraction from the original claims of their case. The allegations came as part of a filing in an ongoing lawsuit that Apple brought against OpenAI in July, alleging the AI company stole the iPhone maker’s trade secrets to develop its own gadgets. Apple alleged in its original filing that former employees who went to work for OpenAI downloaded confidential files, and urged job candidates to bring Apple parts to interviews at OpenAI. OpenAI has denied the claims, saying Apple hasn’t been able to identify any stolen trade secrets and has sought to dismiss the case. Both companies are racing to create AI-enabled devices. This week, Apple announced HomeView, its biggest push into the smart home market in nearly a decade with a revamped version of Siri, making it a critical piece of Apple’s AI strategy. OpenAI is working on an AI-enabled device, reported to be a small screen-free smart speaker. Last year, OpenAI brought on former Apple product design chief Jonny Ive and his company, io, to take over design and creative responsibilities across the company. While engineers and researchers regularly switch companies in Silicon Valley, Apple said in a court filing that OpenAI has hired more than 400 of its former employees. CNN’s Lisa Eadicicco contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: Pope Leo’s cancer diagnosis shocked the Vatican — what comes next for the papacy?
cnn.com.text: Thousands of people congregated in the Vatican’s St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday for a Mass that Pope Leo should have been presiding over. Instead, another senior Catholic Church official took his place, while the first American pope recovered in a hospital after being diagnosed with lung cancer following an operation to remove a lobe of his right lung. The pope’s cancer diagnosis, confirmed on Tuesday, has caused alarm across the Catholic world. Pope Leo was elected less than 18 months ago at the age of 69, the youngest man chosen to lead the Catholic Church since Pope John Paul II almost 40 years earlier. Given his relatively youthful age, the view in the Vatican and among church leaders was that Leo had a long papacy in front of him. That assumption is now being tested. The era of papal health struggles had, many in the Vatican hoped, been put aside in the short term. Leo’s predecessor Pope Francis, elected at 76 and with part of his right lung missing, had a series of health problems towards the end of his pontificate, and spent weeks in the Gemelli hospital with pneumonia. Francis, who had served as pope since 2013, died of a stroke and heart failure in April 2025. Pope Leo’s approach to his health has been steady, sensible and balanced. He goes to the papal retreat at Castel Gandolfo outside of Rome every Tuesday for a day off. He plays tennis, he swims, and as a cardinal had a personal trainer. All of that added to the shock of his hospital admission. “No one expected it,” Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Holy See Secretary of State, told reporters, likening it to a “bolt from the blue.” The cardinal, speaking before the cancer diagnosis was confirmed, added: “I am worried.” Leo XIV has cancelled all his audiences until October 20 as he continues his recovery. The doctors are confident that the cancer was removed during surgery, but further tests are needed. For the pope, near term plans are up in the air. Leo went into hospital in the middle of a major Vatican gathering of bishops and church leaders, which he had convened. The discussions focused on how the church can support couples and families a decade on from a major document issued by Pope Francis, which opened the possibility of divorced and remarried Catholics being able to receive communion. The meeting was an example of Leo, in his own style, seeking to implement the reforms begun by his predecessor. But his operation meant he could not take part in the Mass that concluded the gathering or take an active part in the meetings. “It’s very concerning and I think the more recent news that it is actually a cancer is very worrying for everybody,” Archbishop Tim Costelloe, the president of the Australian Bishops’ Conference, said just off St Peter’s Square following the Mass on Wednesday. The archbishop had been taking part in the gathering and said he’d written to the pope on behalf of his country’s bishops assuring him of prayers and support. Questions are being asked of future papal travel. From Nov. 6-17, the pope is due to be in Latin America for an intense three country tour to Uruguay, Argentina and an emotional “homecoming” to Peru, where he served as a missionary and bishop. His packed itinerary includes 14 flights, 50 events and visits to some high-altitude parts of the continent. Archbishop Costelloe says the latest developments “inevitably” raise questions about the forthcoming trip, but stressed Leo is “a strong man, he’s a fit man” and there was plenty of hope he “can get past this.” As of Wednesday, no changes have been announced to the dates of the trip. Leo XIV, a meticulous and details-oriented leader, made sure everything was in order before his operation. A couple of days before announcing he was going in for surgery, the pope confirmed the election of Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, a high-ranking Vatican official from the Philippines, to the important role of Dean of the College of Cardinals. This is the position held by the fictional Cardinal Lawrence played by Ralph Fiennes in the movie “Conclave,” released in the months before the real-life papal election that chose Leo. The appointment of Tagle, who stood in for Leo to preside at Wednesday’s mass at the Vatican, has acquired a new significance with the pope in the hospital. The dean, who is the “first among equals” leader of the college, plays a crucial role in presiding over a conclave (providing he’s under 80) and the pre-conclave meetings. Any future papal election is considered far into the future. But the appointment of the 69-year-old Tagle, a charismatic figure previously tipped as a possible pope, was an important piece of housekeeping. Leo’s cancer diagnosis has been met by an outpouring of public support. It offers an opportunity for him to connect with so many other individuals and families who have been affected by the illness. “Pope Leo has shown compassionate solidarity with so many people encountering struggles and challenges in their lives,” Fr. Joseph Farrell, the leader of the Augustinian religious order and a friend of the pope, told CNN. “As Augustinians, we invite all people to show that same loving, prayerful solidarity with the Holy Father.” Leo is an Augustinian and a former leader of the order. There is a history of cancer in the pope’s family, with his eldest brother Louis Prevost currently being treated for the illness, which he was first diagnosed with in 2017. The pope’s mother, Mildred, died of cancer in 1990. His father, also Louis, died of colon cancer and heart disease in 1997. While inside the Vatican there is worry about his health, the cogs of the church’s central administration will keep on turning. “It’s not a case of running around pulling hair out,” one official told CNN. “We are getting on with the work inside the dicasteries (Vatican departments) which support the pope’s ministry.” And the pope can still govern the church from his hospital bed. Those who know the pope well say he will be keen to bounce back. Elise Allen, who interviewed the pope in July 2025 for her book on Leo XIV, described the situation as a “waiting game” but it was important not to jump to too many conclusions. “He’s a very hard worker, he’s very determined, he’s going to want to get back into the swing of things very quickly if that’s possible,” she told CNN. Allen said, however, that his hospitalization may lead him to “scale back” some of his appointments and commitments. She also pointed out that his last major health crisis, as a young missionary sent to Peru, was definitive. In 1985, soon after arriving in the country, Leo was struck down with Typhoid fever. Allen said that it was a turning point as, following his recovery, it led him to embrace his work in South America. Both popes John Paul II and Francis show how the role of pontiff involves an element of public suffering. And as recent conclaves have elected men in their late 60s and 70s, health difficulties are never far around the corner. “Fragility deserves special attention,” Leo XIV said in his speech to the family life gathering last week. “The experience of families has something to teach everyone, since fragility belongs to our common human condition and therefore also to the life of the Church.” The pope is now embracing that same fragility and uncertainty that many others with a similar diagnosis have faced.

cnn.com.title: Exclusive: Judge limited Justice Department access to Rep. Ilhan Omar’s records in sprawling immigration fraud probe
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration pushed for an unusually aggressive search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s house in recent days in an immigration fraud probe that targets the congresswoman, possible false statements made on government documents, and a potential conspiracy, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation. Prosecutors, however, first had to contend with a federal magistrate judge, in a prolonged back-and-forth that hasn’t previously been reported. Judge Matthew Sharbaugh of the DC District Court ultimately limited how the Justice Department could access Omar’s documents in Monday’s search, before he would approve the warrant, because of her role as a member of Congress and the Constitutional protections that affords, multiple people familiar with the investigation told CNN. The investigators’ inquiries that prompted the search include whether Omar or her now-deceased father lied about her age when she obtained citizenship in 2000, claiming she was a minor when she was of adult age. Omar emigrated to the US as a Somalian refugee around the age of 12 and became a citizen in 2000, according to people familiar with Omar’s situation. One source told CNN the government could try to expand the investigation into a wider conspiracy case and try to investigate if this was deception and the purposeful falsification of information over years by a larger group of individuals. Omar has been under criminal investigations for years — including before Trump took office last year. But the Trump administration has pushed further with the belief that she has repeated false statements when filling out government documents, such as a passport, in recent years. That is what led to the search on Monday, the sources say. The search of her home in DC was highly unusual for its timing less than a month before Election Day voting ends, including while Omar is running for reelection as a Democrat in Minnesota. The federal push this month has also been unusual for its attempt to access a member of Congress’ records — the type of criminal investigative work that Republicans this year have made into a political firestorm for past administrations. As part of the renewed probe, at least a dozen subpoenas were issued beginning last Friday to witnesses, most of them relatives, according to people familiar with the investigation. Government records and archives in Somalia are notoriously unreliable and hard to access due to years of conflict and disconnected government entities. Judge limits search on Omar’s home In recent weeks, the Justice Department argued for broad access to records that Omar kept at her home in Washington, the sources said. The Justice Department has argued that with Omar there was little need for sequestering the records taken from her home on Monday. But the judge who ultimately approved the search told the Justice Department that wasn’t possible under the law, the sources said. Sharbaugh of the DC District Court told prosecutors from DC they would need to set up a process for screening the records to protect Omar’s legislative work from investigators. In DC, the courts have upheld expansive protections around records of legislative work for members of Congress under the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause. The multi-day back-and-forth between the judge and the Justice Department in recent days hasn’t been previously reported. It may now have vast implications for both federal investigators that are looking to potentially charge Omar with a crime and for her campaign. The Justice Department’s approach to the search also was especially notable because Omar, a US citizen originally from Somalia, is a high-profile member of the group of female progressives known as “The Squad,” a top and frequent political target of President Donald Trump and is running for re-election to Congress in Minnesota, where voting in the mid-term elections has already begun. Omar has publicly called the search of her home a political attack prompted by the hatred that Trump and Republicans have for her. “This is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar said in a post on social media on Monday. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” She has denied any wrongdoing and hasn’t been charged with a crime. An attorney for Omar didn’t respond to multiple requests for this story. Years of investigations into Omar Investigators are looking into an unsubstantiated claim around whether her now ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, was her brother, in order to get him citizenship — a claim that has been repeated by Trump and which Omar has called “bigoted lies.” Even if substantiated, the statute of limitations would have long run out over any crime, and it’s unclear what role that would play in the inquiry, informed sources told CNN. No charges were brought by the Biden-era investigators and the case around Omar didn’t progress nearly as far as the current Trump-era investigators have taken it, several people familiar with the investigation said. The case was reopened last year and is now being led by prosecutors in the deputy attorney general’s office and in the US attorney’s office in Minneapolis, the sources said. The US Attorney’s Office in Washington, DC, has also been involved. Any new case, if charged, would likely be complicated by Trump’s rhetoric against Omar, over many years and some of it being racist. Vice President JD Vance has also talked about discussing the case with White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, and White House border czar Tom Homan has repeatedly talked on Fox News about an ongoing investigation into Omar. “If someone committed immigration violation, someone committed marriage fraud or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law, so I’ll leave it at that,” Homan said in a September interview after mentioning an “ongoing criminal investigation” around Omar. A separate investigation of possible financial misconduct, including around campaign finance, also continues in the DC US attorney’s office. DC US Attorney Jeanine Pirro was asked on Tuesday on Fox News about Omar’s financial disclosures that House ethics investigators previously scrutinized. “That is the subject of an investigation as well,” Pirro said. “We’re looking at the facts. Based upon the facts we will follow them wherever they take us.” Since the DC federal court’s oversight of the search of Omar’s home, any criminal investigation that would rely on her own records may be slowed down substantially, and has already raised concerns about Justice Department integrity and politicization. Judges in the DC District Court have grown increasingly skeptical of the Trump administration’s approach to Constitutional protections in criminal cases, especially when those cases appear politically charged. At the same time, Republicans have been furious with the Justice Department under President Joe Biden for seeking Congress members’ communications in past criminal investigations. Republicans on Capitol Hill and Trump have been particularly critical of former special counsel Jack Smith obtaining secrecy orders when Smith’s office subpoenaed phone companies for call logs of members around the January 6, 2021, US Capitol attack conspiracy investigation. Generally, the Justice Department avoids overt investigative activity that could affect an election within 60 days of Election Day. In this case, however, top Justice officials signed off on Monday’s HSI search.

cnn.com.title: Zelensky says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian refineries as frustration with Trump mounts
cnn.com.text: Ukraine will resume strikes on Russia’s oil refineries President Volodymyr Zelensky has said, also criticizing what he called a “dangerous” withdrawal of US intelligence sharing and restrictions to the Starlink satellite internet service. The Ukrainian leader said he had halted attacks on Russian oil infrastructure for three days after the US announced a surprise “energy ceasefire” initiative. But given that Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities continued, Zelensky told the Financial Times: “We’re done.” On Thursday, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Ukraine had attempted a large-scale attack on a Russian oil refinery in Ryazan overnight. Ukraine has not yet commented. Zelensky’s comments lay bare his growing frustration with President Donald Trump, who last week announced a controversial deal to buy Russian diesel. Trump has heaped pressure on Ukraine to stop striking Moscow’s refineries as he works to bring down energy costs ahead of the midterm elections. Zelensky has condemned Trump’s willingness to strike business deals with Moscow as well as the US president’s apparent admiration for Russia’s Vladimir Putin. He also told the FT that Ukrainian military officials were told by their US counterparts that “if you will not stop [the energy strikes], we will block intelligence.” Then on Wednesday, Ukraine said Starlink had restricted some military internet services, disrupting key operations, deepening alarm in both Kyiv and among European allies. Last week, Trump wrote on social media that Russia’s President Vladimir Putin agreed to supply markets with his country’s diesel fuel as the US president works to bring down energy costs. That move drew bipartisan criticism and sparked anger among European allies. On Monday, Russian forces launched fresh attacks on Ukraine just hours after the US president stated an “energy ceasefire” had come into effect – a measure that neither Moscow nor Kyiv had publicly confirmed. Both Russian and Ukrainian troops intensified aerial attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure in the weeks leading up to that as movements on the battlefield remain relatively stagnant. The Trump administration had warned Ukraine and allies in Europe that the US could suspend intelligence sharing and European purchases of US weapons for Kyiv if it did not halt deep strikes on Russian energy facilities. Information sharing is invaluable to Ukrainian defense efforts against Russian ballistic missile attacks by giving the locations of missile launchers along with data on where the strikes are being directed, and when. In the days that followed, Trump administration officials, including the president, insisted such intelligence sharing continued. But what explained the lack of missile warnings? When asked by Kyiv for an explanation, US officials blamed the weather. But Ukrainian officials suspected it was deliberate. “America says it was a failure,” a European official told CNN. “But it can’t be the truth.” “This will give Russians a real leverage on a frontline at the time when we effectively stopped their advances, and de-occupy the territories,” a Ukrainian official told CNN. Defensive capabilities ‘artificially restricted’ That information deficit has been compounded by Elon Musk’s Starlink curbing some internet services in Ukraine, according to local officials. Ukrainian authorities said they were caught off-guard by restrictions on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink, called Starshield. A Ukrainian Defense Ministry Source told CNN on Thursday that “as of now, Starshield’s operations have resumed and are continuing.” The source added that the ministry is talking with all parties involved “to determine all the causes and circumstances of yesterday’s restrictions.” But Zelensky has indicated that some restrictions are still in place. On Thursday morning, the Ukrainian president said Russia had launched more than 850 attack drones since midnight “at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted.” Zelensky said earlier that Ukrainian forces use the satellite system to defend against Moscow’s jet-powered Shahed drones, and that Russia was trying to capitalize on the disruptions. Musk on Wednesday said Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government and that any limits on its speed or usage are up to the US military and president. He added that Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX and is limited to civilian or defensive activities. Musk said Starlink “cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.” CNN has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment. Zelensky has spent the past week trying to shore up support among European leaders. On Wednesday, he met Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles in London.

cnn.com.title: Sally Rooney’s books no longer sold in UK over support for banned pro-Palestinian group
cnn.com.text: Irish novelist Sally Rooney’s books will no longer be sold in Britain over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine ​Action, a pro-Palestinian group banned as a terrorist organisation, Rooney and ‌her publisher said on Wednesday. The bestselling author, known for novels including “Normal People” and “Conversations with Friends,” has been a vocal supporter of Palestine Action, including after it was proscribed by ​the British government under terrorism laws last year. Rooney previously said in ​a witness statement submitted to London’s High Court, in support of ⁠a legal challenge over the ban on Palestine Action, that her plans ​could lead to her books being withdrawn from sale in Britain. Her publisher Faber ​said on Wednesday that it had agreed with Rooney that “we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format,” though it would sell her works elsewhere. “Current ​legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass ​on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work,” Faber said in a statement. “To sell ‌a ⁠writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.” Rooney said in a statement: “I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions and I ​am wholly prepared to ​accept the ⁠consequences.” Palestine Action, which had increasingly targeted Israel-linked defense companies, was banned shortly after a June 2025 break-in at the ​Royal Air Force’s Brize Norton base. Last year, Palestine Action’s co-founder ​Huda Ammori ⁠challenged the ban and the High Court ruled in her favor in February, before the Court of Appeal overturned that decision in June. The Supreme Court is due ⁠to ​hear an appeal next month. More than 3,000 people ​have since been arrested for holding signs in support of Palestine Action and its proscription has ​been criticized by civil liberties groups.

cnn.com.title: Pope shares first message after lung cancer diagnosis
cnn.com.text: Pope Leo XIV thanked fellow Catholics for their prayers on Wednesday in his first message since he underwent surgery for lung cancer in Rome. “As you know, I have been unable to be among you during these days,” Leo wrote in a statement to Catholics participating in a symposium for the 10th anniversary of Amoris laetitia, a document written by his predecessor Pope Francis on the church’s work with couples and families. “I thank you warmly for your prayers and for the work you have done together. Your sharing of experiences and attentive listening are indeed a gift to the whole Church,” he said. “I ask you please to pray for me, as I pray for you.” Leo was diagnosed with pulmonary adenocarcinoma, a common type of lung cancer, during a 90-minute surgery in Rome yesterday wherein doctors removed the lower lobe of one of his lungs, according to medical staff who treated the pontiff. The pope’s recovery is “proceeding as expected,” Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora said in their statement. Leo was able to walk around his quarters in the hospital, and the Vatican’s spokesperson said Wednesday the pontiff jointly conducted mass with other priests in a room specially set up on his floor. The pope announced his planned surgery in a speech over the weekend to faithful in St. Peter’s Square, saying that the “growth” on his lung was found at an early stage. The pope isn’t known to be a smoker and has made efforts to have a healthy lifestyle, but there is a history of cancer in his immediate family. His older brother Louis Prevost is currently in treatment for cancer, and their parents died of the disease in the 1990s. Pope Leo has cancelled all his public appearances until October 20 in light of his treatment, though he is due to embark on a long trip to South America next month.

cnn.com.title: Gift for Putin as fears grow that Trump is turning the screws on Ukraine
cnn.com.text: Ultimately, you have to wonder what it is that Vladimir Putin says to Donald Trump when they are on the phone. A week ago, a call between the US president and his Russian counterpart seemed to be about an urgent clarification over a possible outbreak of plague in Siberia. Instead, a controversial deal to buy Russian diesel emerged, prompting fury from Ukrainians, and then Trump demanding they get a new president. For days, fears grew across Europe this may spill into the real world of the US limiting military aid and intelligence for Ukraine, and in the past 48 hours, that might be spilling into reality. Twice now, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has declared Kyiv was not given the usual warning about Russian ballistic missile attacks from its partners. The US, whose satellites and other methods are the early warning mechanisms for Russian launches, normally provide Ukrainians a vital few minutes to run to the shelter before the missiles hit. Thirty-nine slammed into Ukraine last night. President Trump has openly rejected the idea he has stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, saying Tuesday: “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel.” But that does not preclude the possibility less intelligence is being shared, or it is less in real time. With the dead from Russian strikes often in the dozens, as Moscow seeks to yet further widen the envelope of what civilian carnage it will impose, a sudden withdrawal of these early warnings would mean many Ukrainians will likely die. It is possible there is another reason for Zelensky’s messaging – that he is pre-emptively posturing, or that poor weather or technical issues prompted the lack of warnings. The second withdrawal of assistance that appeared to beset Ukraine Wednesday also suggests Trump is squeezing them harder. Starlink space-based internet antennae – assisting Ukrainian medium and longer-range drones to hit their targets, and interceptors to tackle Russian loitering drones – have had significant speed limits imposed on them. This may amount to the removal of a bonus capability negotiated by the former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov with Space X’s owner, Elon Musk. It is important to note it is not comparable to Musk’s decision to entirely stop Starlink functioning inside Russia, which significantly hampered Moscow’s frontline operations in the summer of last year. But it is a palpable snub with operational significance, and one that Ukrainian officials have said would only have occurred at the behest of the White House. For days, European and Ukrainian officials have warned the US was threatening to limit intelligence and other cooperation if Kyiv did not stop hitting Russian diesel facilities. Trump has – somewhat misleadingly – stated Ukrainian targeting of Moscow’s oil facilities is behind a surge in pump prices in the United States, choosing to ignore the role the Strait of Hormuz has played in this global economic calamity. It is possible the Starlink slowdown and lack of ballistic warnings shows this threat coming to life. President Trump has denied this is the case, but that is not in of itself definitive proof it is not happening. Trump has also – since he spoke to Putin – again swung from deciding to finally allow Ukraine to build its own Patriot interceptors, a high-profile and vital move long-prevaricated over, to deciding the true obstacle to peace is Zelensky, the president of the invaded country, who has been asking for an immediate ceasefire for over a year. It does not appear to influence Trump’s thought process when Putin attacks Ukrainian energy facilities in the middle of Trump’s self-declared “energy ceasefire.” Or when Putin’s operatives plot to murder a dissident in Washington DC. Or when US businesses are relentlessly hit in Ukraine. There are moments when Trump simply appears bent on hurting Ukraine and damaging its position. We may never learn why, or what it is that Putin says to him to cause this relatively frequent flip in Trump’s worldview. Conjecture might revive the old trope that Trump the real-estate dealmaker seeks to pressure his subcontractors (here, Ukraine) to get the deal to go through or forge a price more palatable to his end consumer (Putin), who he has correctly assessed is in the driving seat of the war and therefore any peace deal. But the timing of this pressure rarely comes when a deal is close, or appears supported by logic. Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel, by most analysis, won’t impact prices at the American pump before the mid-terms, but will likely flood the Kremlin’s coffers with badly needed cash. Zelensky and his European allies have seen this vacillation enough times to be inured to its emotional impact, and perhaps even relaxed about how long it might sustain. Perhaps more Trump-whispering by France’s Macron, or another call from NATO’s Rutte, or visit from Italy’s Meloni, will see the US president flip back again. Indeed, Zelensky was in London Wednesday, and the topic has surely come up. But Trump’s persistent sympathy for Russia’s position remains a mystery of our time. Critics say it is unlikely to achieve his apparent goal of a peace deal, incompatible with the long-term security interests of the United States, and oblivious to Moscow’s role in assisting Iran , which continues to embarrass Trump and injure American servicemen. There is an inherent risk in the current state of affairs, however, to both Trump and Putin. First, Trump might create such acrimony in his transatlantic relationships, that his allies simply zone him out for the 18 months after the mid-terms, and wait for him to depart. That could leave Trump further hamstrung when dealing with an intractable conflict, spreading in the Middle East. There is risk for Putin too. Europe and Ukraine being forced to forge ahead without the United States, fashion resilience, find new methods, and surge funding into their defense, does not leave the Kremlin in a dominant position. The more Moscow antagonizes Europe, the more it arms up, and the greater, in the long-term, the (defensive) threat Europe’s armies pose to Russia. Ukraine has shown extraordinary inventiveness and capability. That is unlikely to stop, and likely to again reshape the landscape of warfare in the coming years. Similarly, Russia’s capacity to absorb pain is immense. Yet its breaking point is rarely publicly visible, and tends to surge menacingly from the deep without warning, as when the frustrated chief of Russia’s infamous Wagner mercenary force launched a short-lived rebellion in 2023. In the immediate term however, the risk of this current strategy is born entirely by Ukraine. Its children and mothers are dying from nightly strikes. Its cities are sleepless. And its military aid is prey to two powerful men’s curious bromance.

cnn.com.title: Democrats have reason to be optimistic, but headaches could be waiting if they win the midterms
cnn.com.text: If Democrats win the Senate next month, the chamber’s new swing voters will likely be an interesting cast. They’ll be Democrats from states that voted for President Donald Trump by double digits, and who have distanced themselves from their party on transgender rights, oil drilling, immigration and even the left’s desire to scrutinize the Trump administration. And some of them are anxious to tout their willingness to work with the president. Democratic leaders did a good job recruiting and helping nominate candidates with moderate brands whom voters seem to like. That’s helped them compete on a difficult map where the party needs to win at least two states Trump won by double digits to nab the majority. But if Democrats nab that majority, the party will face a challenge in trying to balance the interests of some of these new moderate lawmakers with the demands of the base. One of the most common issues where these moderate candidates have tacked to the right has been transgender athletes. Opposition to allowing transgender students to play on girls’ sports teams — or some version of that position — has been embraced by state Rep. Josh Turek in Iowa, state Rep. James Talarico in Texas, pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas and physician Annie Andrews in South Carolina. Both Talarico and Andrews had previously embraced a broader version of transgender rights and spoke out on behalf of that community. But after Trump attacked Andrews using an anti-transgender slur, the South Carolina Democrat filmed a direct-to-camera ad in which she said, “I don’t support biological men playing women’s sports and I don’t support — and haven’t ever performed — gender surgery for minors.” She added in a debate on Sunday: “I don’t support gender surgery on minors.” Hamilton added the same day on ABC’s “This Week”: “I believe that there are two biological genders.” Another significant break from the national party has been on immigration. “Democrats have failed on the border,” Andrews said at the debate. Talarico has said that “Joe Biden and his administration failed us on our southern border.” Alaska Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola has run an ad touting her votes breaking with her party on the border, including being one of just six House Democrats to symbolically condemn then-Vice President Kamala Harris and the Biden administration’s border policies in 2024. Turek has also repeatedly returned to that theme, including launching a new ad this week featuring a sheriff saying Turek “broke with his party and voted with Republicans to support law enforcement … and crack down on illegal immigration.” He indeed voted with just a few Democrats to make being in the country illegally a state crime in Iowa. Other areas of separation are a bit more state specific. One of Peltola’s big issues is increased oil and gas production. The Alaska Democrat also touts her “A” rating from the National Rifle Association. Hamilton has also decried the “war on domestic energy projects” The Kansas Democrat even said he’d consider a temporary diesel export ban, which Trump floated and then later ruled out, to hopefully lower prices (despite experts being skeptical of the idea). And Hamilton also recently suggested he’s not overly keen on some Democrats’ desire to investigate Trump administration officials — saying he instead prefers to institute “guardrails.” “I’m not going to Washington to hold trials,” he told MS NOW. “I’m going to Washington to fight for the people of Kansas and make life better for them.” That could seemingly be a problem if that kind of accountability becomes a major focus for a potential Democratic majority. (That would likely be where much of Democrats’ energy is devoted since it’s not as if they will be able to pass a far-ranging agenda with Trump still in office.) At the same time, however, we don’t necessarily know how these situations will pan out. Just because Hamilton says holding trials won’t be his focus, that doesn’t necessarily mean he would oppose his party’s move toward that or other accountability from Trump officials. Many of these Democrats are breaking with their party in potentially symbolic ways: They’re staking out a rhetorical difference without necessarily indicating that they would vote against the party on major issues that are likely to come up over the next two years. There is some evidence that Americans have warmed to the Democratic Party as these kinds of candidates have led the charge. A Gallup poll this week showed the party’s favorable rating rising to 43% — up from the mid-30s last year and 8 points higher than Republicans’ favorability. And the percentage of Americans who said the Democratic Party is “too liberal” has declined from 55% in 2022 to 46% today. But if Democrats do win either or both chambers in Congress, that new power could embolden the party’s left flank to try and assert themselves, leading to potential clashes within the party. To some degree, that’s the new reality for Democrats. There are simply more red states than blue states these days, and Trump won 24 of the 50 states by double digits. So if Democrats don’t run the table in swing states, they need to run moderate candidates who can win in pretty red territory. But that won’t make dealing with that tension any easier. Many in the party’s base have agonized over the sway that moderate former Democratic senators like Joe Manchin of West Virginia and Kyrsten Sinema of Arizona had as swing votes — and that Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman could have come next year. And there could be more where that came from.

cnn.com.title: Trump was trying to force prices lower ahead of the midterms. But Iran gets a vote, too
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump and Republicans just got the worst news on inflation ahead of the midterms: Prices rose more than expected in September. The news came as no surprise to American voters. Polls show they’re furious about the high cost of living that has persisted since the pandemic but has been exacerbated this year by Trump’s policies – including tariffs and, primarily, the Iran war. To alleviate some of the price pain, the Trump administration has been diving deep into its bag of tricks. Over a month ago, the US Navy began a high-stakes effort to assist tankers shuttling Gulf oil out of the Strait of Hormuz. And in a hail-Mary attempt, Trump last week announced a controversial deal to drop some sanctions on Russia to import a relatively small amount of the country’s diesel. Iran and its Houthi allies are now undermining both of those operations. An increase in attacks on tankers and oil infrastructure over the past week has sent oil and diesel prices higher. The disruption has sent transits through the straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb falling sharply after mostly recovering to their pre-war levels. The Trump administration was never going to solve the inflation problem in the month leading up to the midterms. But its last-ditch effort for some positive news on prices has run face-first into a brick wall this week. Inflation Wednesday’s Consumer Price Index showed a familiar story: Inflation continued to rise in September, boosted mostly by surging energy costs. Gas prices rose 9.1% over the course of the month and ended September more than 34% higher than the same time last year. Fuel oil prices rose 15.3% last month and surged more than 74% over the course of the past year. Those higher costs are starting to spread to other parts of the economy. As my colleague Matt Egan noted Tuesday, the Iran war is costing the average American household $2,000 in additional costs, according to Moody’s Analytics. Particularly concerning in Wednesday’s inflation report was the surprising rebound in housing and rent costs, a significant contributor to inflation that had cooled off in the spring and summer. All services rose 0.4% in the month – prices that tend to rise as yoga studios, lawn services and the like charge their customers more to make up for their rising costs. Those services prices may only be a knock-on effect from the Iran war, but economists get worried when they rise, because they tend to be “sticky.” Bluntly: When was the last time your kids’ nursery school lowered prices? The overall US economy remains hot and consumers keep spending despite rising prices. But higher inflation has translated into higher bond yields and rates from the Federal Reserve, which are lifting borrowing costs and making housing even less affordable. The Strait of Hormuz Iran knows all this. It knows the political pressure Trump and his Republican party are facing. And it knows what month it is. After a relatively quiet September, at least 18 vessels in and around the Middle East have been attacked over the past two weeks, according to Kpler, a maritime tracking service. On Tuesday, the Iran-allied Houthis appeared to hit the headquarters of Saudi state oil giant Aramco. “It appears Iran is attempting to keep oil prices high ahead of the midterm elections, and the best way to do this has been to increase attacks - both from themselves and via the Houthis,” said Matt Smith, analyst at Kpler. The ever-shifting narrative about who controls the Strait of Hormuz has changed once again. The complex operation of naval-protected dark fleets shuttling Gulf oil out of the strait and offloading it to tankers in the Gulf of Oman had been hugely successful. Just a few weeks ago, oil transits out of the Strait of Hormuz had almost fully recovered to their pre-war levels. Over the past seven days, oil and fuel transits through the strait have fallen to 54% of their pre-war levels, according to Kpler. Iran’s retaliation should surprise no one, said Dan Pickering, founder and chief investment officer at Pickering Energy Partners. “As the US trumpets the success of getting more crude out to global markets, it feels somewhat like sporting a big ‘kick me’ sign,” he said. “Iran is attacking almost everyone. Meanwhile, Iran’s proxy, the Houthis, are attacking Saudi Arabia with substantial results.” Recent Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure have raised the stakes of the war. Although the oil market largely dodged a bullet after a successful but repairable attack on Saudi Arabia’s crucial East-West pipeline, the recent attacks prove that the conflict isn’t abating anytime soon. The ultimate winner can’t yet be known: The US Navy may once again gain the upper hand. The administration may find other creative ways to get more diesel flowing to the market. In the meantime, the loser is clear: The American consumer. And in three weeks they will be casting their verdict on the economy as they vote in the midterms.

cnn.com.title: Katie Zacharia presented herself as a lawyer. She’s not
cnn.com.text: The press secretary is supposed to spin the news, not be the news. On that most essential qualification, the new lead White House spokeswoman, Katie Zacharia, is struggling. She has presented herself as a lawyer but does not meet the requirements in her home state to use that title. And at least one watchdog group has asked the State Bar of California to investigate. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing a person with direct knowledge of the matter, that Zacharia failed in an attempt to pass the California bar exam after graduating from law school. Zacharia has a law degree from the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law. She also claims to have worked with appropriate credentials in China, but it’s not at all clear what credential she’s talking about. White House spokesman Steven Cheung defended Zacharia in a statement. “Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team,” he said. “She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary.” These developments are made even more awkward after Republicans mercilessly attacked the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor, though he went to medical school and made his career in public health. Squabbles over who can call themselves a lawyer or a doctor probably seem beside the point to a large portion of the country. This issue here is not that a law degree is required to be White House press secretary — it isn’t. The issue is that Zacharia has presented herself repeatedly on TV, including on CNN, as a lawyer, something the independent journalist Judd Legum first documented. Trump used the term “attorney” to describe her when he announced she would be his press secretary. A review by CNN’s K-File found at least six instances when she referred to herself as either a lawyer or a corporate lawyer in her own words and multiple other instances in which she posted or reposted to social media using the term attorney or “legal strategist.” A town full of law degrees Washington, DC, is filled to the brim with people who have law degrees but do not practice law. And it does not appear that Zacharia inappropriately tried to represent anyone in a court. But all of this does suggest the vetting operation at the White House is, to be charitable, not very thorough. When reporters asked Trump at the White House Tuesday where Zacharia passed the bar, she chimed in from behind him that she was when she moved to China. Even Trump did a double take. She later clarified to The New York Times that she had misheard the question. “I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” she said. “That’s all I could hear over the sound of Marine One,” she added, “and wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question.” Zacharia’s legal work Zacharia later said in a statement she had “practiced international transactional law, with all the appropriate credentials.” On her Linkedin page Zacharia lists herself as having worked as an “associate” in the international practice group at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing for nearly two years starting in 2011. The Journal reported that she was one of four associates working as an “international legal consultant.” Only citizens can become licensed to practice law in China, according to the Ministry of Justice, so it’s not clear what kind of credential she might have obtained. “Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law,” according to a White House official. In addition to saying on TV that she is a lawyer, Zacharia cites some other legal-sounding work on her LinkedIn page; for example, she lists herself as “general counsel” for the activist group Fix California. In the nonprofit group’s tax filing for 2024, Zacharia’s name appears as having been a fundraiser. CNN’s White House team has found no evidence that Zacharia has passed the bar exam in the states where she has lived and worked since graduating from Pepperdine. Here’s what California’s bar association told them: What’s required to be a lawyer in California California law lays out what’s required to be a lawyer. There are requirements for college and law school, or their equivalents; for “good moral character”; passing an ethics exam; and passing the bar exam in California. Zacharia, as a result, should not be considered a lawyer in California, the state where she has lived and worked. A separate section of California law makes it a misdemeanor to pretend to be a lawyer. Here’s the language: Does presenting oneself as a lawyer on TV violate that piece of code? The group Campaign for Accountability, which describes itself as a nonpartisan government watchdog, on Wednesday announced it had asked the State Bar of California to investigate. Trump is his own spokesman. But he’ll need good help None of that really matters to anyone who is more concerned with how the White House is handling the war Trump launched on Iran or the related inflation that continues to hit Americans in the wallet. Questions about whether Zacharia can call herself a lawyer, or not, mostly distract from those other, larger issues. Ultimately, Trump is the person who speaks for his administration in the long, often rambling appearances he frequently makes in the Oval Office. But those appearances may become less enjoyable for him in the future, especially if Democrats take control of one or both chambers of Congress and, as expected, launch a series of investigations into his administration, the money his family has made during his presidency, and much more. He will, at that point, need a press secretary he can trust. Republicans have questioned Abdul El-Sayed’s credentials Questions about Zacharia’s CV are also an awkward development since Republicans in Michigan have attacked the Democrat running for Senate there, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor despite having gone to medical school. At a debate this month, the Republican in the Senate race, former Rep. Mike Rogers, went so far as to say El-Sayed was a “con man.” As CNN has reported, El-Sayed earned a Doctor of Medicine from Columbia University, but he does not practice clinical medicine. El-Sayed has held public health positions in the Detroit area. His top policy issue is extending health insurance to all Americans. Democratic boosters of El-Sayed have continued to call him a doctor. “Abdul’s a doctor, and he’s taken on special interests to fight for good jobs, better healthcare, and lower costs,” former President Barack Obama said in an ad he cut for the Michigander. CNN’s Kit Maher and Andrew Kaczynski contributed reporting. This headline and story have been updated with additional reporting.

cnn.com.title: Trump administration escalates voter roll fight with threats against California election officials
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration threatened to take legal action against California election officials if they did not review a list of alleged noncitizens on Los Angeles’ voter rolls within 48 hours, according to Tuesday letters from the Justice Department obtained by CNN. The letters, signed by the number two official at the Justice Department, are an escalation in DOJ’s attempts to press for aggressive voter purges with ballots already mailed out in some states, after courts have repeatedly pushed back at attempts by the administration to insert itself in the running of elections. It’s the latest step in a government-wide push to find voter fraud amid President Donald Trump’s baseless claims of widespread cheating in elections. The Justice Department is demanding that the election officials refuse to send ballots to the alleged noncitizen voters and is requesting that election officials segregate ballots from voters on the list until their citizenship is confirmed. Acting deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter wrote in the letters to the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder and the California Secretary of State that if election officials do not take steps to identify the alleged noncitizen voters, DOJ would “have no choice but to seek emergency relief.” McCotter wrote that the department provided a password-protected thumb drive containing names the administration “believes are likely non-citizens” who were sent a mail ballot this year. It requests that the election officials work with the Department of Homeland Security to comply with its demands. The letters were first reported by Reuters. Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said in a statement Wednesday that his office was reviewing the DOJ letter in coordination with California’s secretary of state and attorney general. Logan said that his office had not accessed the thumb drive provided by the federal government “because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols.” The password for the thumb drive was handwritten on what appeared to be a blue post-it note attached to the bottom of the letter sent to Logan’s office on Tuesday. “We do not consider the device a secure medium,” he said. “Additionally, the letter does not specify the number of individuals involved or describe the information contained in the records.” A spokesperson for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber did not immediately respond to CNN’s inquiries. It is not clear what legal avenue the administration could use to force California election officials to take the actions it seeks. The Constitution gives states the primary job of running elections, though it allows Congress to pass some regulations of the vote as well. Earlier this summer, the Justice Department sent letters warning it would prosecute election officials who did not take adequate steps to remove noncitizens from voter registration files, but state officials of both parties dismissed the threat. It’s unclear why the Justice Department sent the letter now, as election officials view the window for changing protocols as closed. “California’s voter lists are public, and this administration has had 21 months with total control of the federal government to review those public lists,” said David Becker, a former DOJ voting section attorney who now advises election administrators. “California sent out mail ballots to all voters on Oct 5. One must question why the DOJ would violate its own rules about investigating elections close to Election Day, and over a week after they knew the state had already mailed ballots out, particularly when their past claims have been full of errors,” Becker said. The Justice Department defended sending the letters. “Federal law is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. The Department will take all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure compliance with federal law,” said DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels. The Trump administration has alleged there are hundreds of thousands of non-citizens on voter rolls. In August, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed DHS had identified 250,000 non-citizens registered to vote in four states — including California, along with Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Nevada — by comparing public voter rolls with federal immigration records. But those claims have come under immense scrutiny and, in some cases, failed to hold up. In Nevada, for instance, DHS acknowledged to state officials that its initial claim of 15,900 non-citizen registrants was an unvetted preliminary finding, and that it had only “confirmed” 185 of them through manual review. Last month, Nevada officials told DHS that their own subsequent review found all 185 were citizens — a conclusion DHS disputes. The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division has also sought unredacted state voter roll data from the states as part of its hunt for noncitizens on the rolls. The department has sued 30 states demanding the data — but lost every case where a judge has ruled so far, including in California. Other attempts by the administration to police how states handle elections have also been shut down in court. The Supreme Court blocked a Trump directive for the US Postal Service to screen mail ballots, and a 2025 executive order from the president seeking to boost the proof of citizenship requirements for voter registration was halted in court as well. Trump’s efforts to implement those requirements through legislation faltered in Congress this year. A recent judge’s ruling dismissing a non-citizen voter prosecution the administration brought in Florida also has raised constitutional questions about the federal law barring non-citizen voting. The administration did secure a major legal win when the Supreme Court okayed a federal immigration data system that Trump has encouraged states to use to vet the citizenship status of their registered voters. Election officials in more than half of the states use the system voluntarily. However, even Republican election officials have balked at proposals from Justice Department that would force them to purge voters whom the administration has deemed ineligible — particularly given the accuracy concerns around the federal government’s data tools. This article has been updated with additional information.

bbc.com.title: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.
For Ukraine, it is vital for communications on the battlefield and effective drone warfare.
Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones can stay connected to operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming.
But on Tuesday night, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield "missions", a top Ukrainian official said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.
The restriction at 100mph (160km/h) meant that any drone travelling faster than that lost connection and was effectively useless.
"Starlink gives Ukraine the ability to see what's coming, to protect people," Kurt Volker, former US ambassador to Nato, told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme. "If you cut that off, then more people are going to get killed - and that is a very cynical and callous decision to slow that down the way that has been done."
Connectivity had been restored by Wednesday evening.
The move has once again shown how Starlink can impact the conflict, which has been raging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
What are Starlink and Starshield?
Starlink is an internet network that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields.
It currently relies on more than 10,000 active satellites, making Starlink the world's largest satellite constellation.
It is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and is the company's biggest revenue driver.
While Starlink is for civilian use, Starshield is its military-grade sister service, designed for the Pentagon.
Starshield relies on the Starlink network, but has greater security like enhanced encryption so that sensitive information can be transmitted without interception.
The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.
How does Starlink work on a battlefield?
Put simply, Starlink uses its thousands of satellites to ping high-speed internet back to almost every corner of the globe, using terminals on the ground that users can easily buy and set up themselves. As Musk said, they have two instructions: "point at sky, plug in".
This makes them ideal for use on the battlefield.
"It's a connection… that you can basically use pretty fast, you don't need any special equipment, you don't need to prepare, you just go to the field and usually it works," Neo, a soldier with one of Ukraine's drone reconnaissance units, told the Today programme.
"It simplifies our work because we can translate or stream our reconnaissance operations," he added.
The network has become "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", George Barros from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.
In Ukraine, both Starlink (the civilian service) and Starshield (the military service) are used, depending on what communications are needed.
It is crucial for the effective use of weapons such as drones, which connect to the network so that operators can see their targets in real time, effectively minimising the time between "sensor-to shooter", Barros told the BBC.
Because Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.
When it comes to Ukraine's self-defence, it relies on the Starlink network to protect its own skies against incoming Russian attacks, especially jet-powered Shahed drones, Barros added.
Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph (319 km/h), meaning the Starlink restriction made Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.
For Neo, this means that any deliberate restrictions on the Starlink network are "a betrayal".
With no ready replacement for the Starlink network, any speed restrictions or loss of connectivity have major implications for Ukraine defences, and the recent limits have shown how dependent Kyiv is on the network.
