theguardian.com.title: Elon Musk suggests US government was behind Starlink restrictions in Ukraine – Europe live
theguardian.com.text:
Morning opening: Musk suggests US government was behind Starlink restrictions
Billionaire tech mogul Elon Musk has suggested that the US government could be behind the decision to restrict the speed of SpaceX’s satellite-technology used by Ukraine’s military.
In a post of X, he appeared to suggest the Trump administration was behind the move, which Ukraine says restricts its ability to use key defensive weapons.
Musk said:
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
In further posts overnight, reacting to Zelenskyy’s comments on his relationship with Donald Trump, Musk went further and appeared to suggest Zelenskyy should leave the post, saying it’s “time to go.”
In a TV interview with Piers Morgan, Zelenskyy said he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s decisions and worried about “losing a strong partner,” playing a critical role across Ukraine’s defence.
For what it’s worth, Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.
The issue is likely to come up again today and tomorrow as EU leaders meet in Brussels for key political talks on the future.
With today’s discussions focused on the bloc’s internal matters, including the EU’s next budget, Ukraine is expected to come up on Friday when Zelenskyy joins other leaders in Brussels. But the ongoing crisis in Ukraine’s relations with the US risks overshadowing the entire meeting.
I will bring you all the updates throughout the day.
It’s Thursday, 15 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
EU leaders heading for mighty clash over EU's next long-term budget - snap analysis
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
One other thing that is clear from this morning’s doorstep statements: leaders are heading for a mighty clash over the EU’s next long-term budget.
Agreeing the EU seven-year budget is always a fraught negotiating exercise, which pits a group of “frugals”, such as Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands, who oppose a bigger budget, against a larger group in southern and eastern Europe, who want to maintain the EU’s traditional spending on agriculture and regional funding.
European Council president António Costa wanted a deal by the end of the year to ensure that the next long-term budget (2028-35) would be ready on time – and avoid getting caught in the crossfire of major elections next year in France, Poland and Italy.
That timing is in doubt, as the EU’s frugals (who prefer to be called “modernisers”) reiterated this morning they are in no hurry.
Sweden’s prime minister Ulf Kristersson said he expected tense talks today.
“We are not reaching agreement this month, not next month. I don’t know even if it’s possible to reach an agreement before the end of the year. I think we are not in a hurry, honestly. We need to have a budget that could combine the modernisation, the resources for Ukraine and of course the traditional things as well. But all the titles [areas of spending] need to be decreased to be able to reach an agreement.”
Friedrich Merz said he expected the “very, very difficult” talks to run into December (11:05) but privately Germany has made it clear it is ready to see the talks go into next year unless there are massive cuts to the current proposal.
In the other camp is Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who described the current proposal as “insufficient” to face the bloc’s challenges, adding that his government would fight to expand it. But with Spain due to hold elections in November, the Socialist leader may not be around to make that argument.
The latest draft summit conclusions call for only a “timely agreement” rather than setting a deadline “by the end of the year”, as in an earlier version.
The European Commission’s €2tn (£1.7tn) budget proposal, which aims to increase spending on defence, border security and research, has already been trimmed by €140bn by Ireland, who as holders of the rotating presidency were tasked with finding a common ground by October.
But almost nobody is happy. The frugal camp thinks the cuts, which target defence and research, are in the wrong places, while the self-styled “friends of cohesion” think there is too much scrimping on the EU’s traditional priorities, such as regional development funds.
France, which does not belong in either camp, but faces acute budget pressures, wants to see the EU agree to new common taxes in order to fund a budget that allows increased spending on new priorities such as defence and maintain the traditional ones, such as farm subsidies.
While the Commission has floated EU taxes on big companies, tobacco and e-waste, member states cannot agree on any of the options.
And the whole budget has to be agreed … by unanimity.
Two drones hit ships in Romanian territorial waters, president Dan says ahead of urgent talks with Nato
Back to Romania, the country’s president Nicușor Dan confirmed that two aerial drone hit ships which caught fire in Romanian territorial waters overnight (12:03).
Dan also said the Romanian state will offer “a reaction” to the incident, without speculating on what it could be. He also suggested that the issue should be added to tomorrow’s agenda on Ukraine-related issues.
Later today, Dan and Bulgaria’s PM Rumen Radev will meet with Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte to discuss the recent incidents in their respective territorial waters.
Swedish parliament rejects Andersson's PM candidacy
A quick update from Sweden, wherethe country’s parliament rejected Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson’s candidacy to form a single-party minority government.
Only 99 lawmakers voted in favour, with 248 against. Two people were absent.
The vote, forced by the parliament’s speaker Andreas Norlén, was widely expected to fail, but is intended to put more pressure on parties as they continue discussions on who could form the next government.
Four centre-left opposition parties, which have all said they favour Andersson as prime minister, won last month a majority of seats in Sweden’s parliament, the Riksdag, but do not agree on who should be part of a new government.
Norlén will now have to appoint a new candidate to hold further exploratory talks on the new government.
'Sanctions must not be lifted,' Zelenskyy says, as he says Russia's attacks come 'in response to signals from US'
Oh, and we have just heard from Zelenskyy again, doubling down on his criticism of Russia and attributing its latest attacks to “signals from the US.”
Responding to a “horrific” drone attack on a supermarket in Odesa, he said:
“Russia continues its bloody terror. The store was partially destroyed, and cars were damaged. Three people were injured. All necessary emergency services are working at the scene and providing assistance to those affected. It is important that our partners help us defend against this. Residential buildings, stores, energy and other critical infrastructure are under attack virtually nonstop. Not a single hour of peace.”
Crucially, he continued:
“What is happening is Russia’s pointed response to the signals it is receiving from America. Unfortunately, there are dangerous signals about the possibility of further sanctions relief. These sanctions were imposed by the world, by America, Europe, and our partners in response to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and its war against us. Nothing has changed. The war has not stopped. The sanctions must not be lifted. Russia must end the slaughter it itself started and has continued for 1,695 days now. More money to fund the killing will not help bring this about. Strength is what is needed, and America is stronger than Russian terror.”
US effort to get Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire collapses
Andrew Roth
in Kyiv
The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after halting those attacks to show that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked the gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.
Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire, the ministry claimed.
In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three and injured six.
“The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement.
'We need honesty from our partners about this war,' Zelenskyy says
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy offered an update on last night’s Russian attacks on Ukraine.
“Emergency services are still providing assistance in dozens of our cities and communities. Repair crews and rescuers are working to deal with the aftermath of Russian attacks. For practically all of yesterday and throughout last night, a massive shahed attack was under way. The drones kept coming in waves, and there was not a single hour when our skies were clear of them.”
He said “more than 850” drones were sent against Ukraine, “at a time when the speed of our defence capabilities is being artificially restricted.”
He added:
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine. Russia exploits every such opportunity and must be held accountable for what it does. Strong decisions are needed to end this war. Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies.
We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security.”
Seven people missing after fire on vessel in Black Sea off Romania
Just as the leaders sit down at the big table in Brussels, Romania has said that seven people are still missing after a fire on a vessel in Romanian territorial waters of the Black Sea.
Suspected Russian drones have hit several ships off Romania and neighbouring Bulgaria since last week in a spillover from the Ukraine war, AFP reported.
Romanian authorities did not say whether a drone caused the fire on the vessel, named as the Wine Trader, which reported a blaze at around 7am, approximately 13 nautical miles southeast of the Romanian city of Sulina.
“Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway,” defence minister Radu Miruță told the Digi24 television channel.
The Romanian Naval Authority said in a statement there were 12 people on board the vessel, AFP reported.
Eight crew were initially reported as missing.
“Five of the sailors on board the Wine Trader have been rescued, a further seven people are still missing,” the Naval Authority said in an update.
EU will voice dismay and 'regret' over the US diesel deal with Russia
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
EU leaders will voice dismay over Donald Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.
“The European Council regrets the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel,” states a draft statement seen by the Guardian to be issued by the 27 leaders when the two-day summit concludes on Friday.
Other leaders, such as Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson, were blunter in their assessment of the deal (9.36).
But EU leaders tread a fine line between their obvious dislike of Trump’s actions towards Russia and dependence on US military support.
That balancing act was epitomised by comments from Estonia’s prime minister, Kristen Michal.
He recalled that the US was one of three Nato nuclear-armed partners supporting his country and described the US as “strong allies” (the others are the UK and France).
He referenced Nato’s help when Estonia faced hybrid attacks and other threats, such as the cutting of cables, Russian fighter jet incursions and drones.
“This kind of help came from Nato and we still have Nato ships on the sea guarding our critical infrastructure. So, [based] on that I must say that Nato is working well and the US is a partner in Nato. And Trump has assured us and everybody else last time in Ankara that he is following Nato and also Article 5 [on collective defence]. So we rely on them – and also sometimes even good friends need a reminder what is right.”
We should put pressure on Russia, not Ukraine, EU's foreign policy chief says
EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas acknowledged that the EU and the US had “definitely different approach to this war,” as she said Europeans believe “we should squeeze Russia, not Ukraine, to surrender and end this war.”
Responding to the US diesel deal with Russia, she said:
“The majority of Russia’s funding for the war comes from oil revenues. Clearly, Ukraine wants this war to stop, and that’s why … cutting off the funding for the war is the way to do it.
We see that we should squeeze … Russia, not Ukraine, to surrender to end this war.”
She added that the EU has adopted a new round of sanction listings earlier this week, as “this is the only way to put pressure on Russia.”
She also said that it’s important to send a clear message to Russia that “all these things they are interested in – [unfreezing] frozen assets, lifting the sanctions – are actually up to Europeans to decide.”
“And these things are not given for free for them,” she said.
Germany's Merz calls for stronger support for Ukraine, but warns of 'very, very difficult' budget talks
Germany’s Friedrich Merz also focused on the budget talks, saying they remain “very, very difficult” and expecting them to run well into December.
On Ukraine, he warned that “we are witnessing an increasingly ruthless wave of attacks by Russia,” and said that “we must do everything possible to support Ukraine not just through the winter, but into next year as well.”
“It remains my firm conviction that we are not merely defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity; we are defending the political order of Europe, which is being subjected to intense pressure by Russia in every respect.”
Hungary’s Péter Magyar focused on other issues in his doorstep statement, particularly on migration and the next EU budget.
But he welcomed the much-awaited law reform in Ukraine that could resolve a longstanding dispute over the rights of the Hungarian minority in western Ukraine, which until now threatened to bloc Kyiv’s accession path.
Magyar will hold a one-on-one with Ukraine’s Zelenskyy tomorrow, his first since ousting Viktor Orbán and coming into power earlier this year.
Ireland's Martin urges Europe to 're-engage' with US, but also calls for 'practical' support for Ukraine with EU accession prospects
Ireland’s Micheál Martin urged Europe to “re-engage” with the US and figure out the best way forward, despite tensions over Ukraine.
“We have had moments in the past when there were challenges and difficulties in respect of this, and it was retrieved by good outreach and engagement from Europe with the US, and I have no doubt that will continue.”
But he said the focus should also be on what the EU can do itself, and that’s primarily to do with advancing Ukraine’s accession process to the bloc.
“I would say to my colleagues across Europe that now is the time to be ambitious over the next number of months to open all clusters in respect of Ukraine and Moldova. The people of Ukraine need that as a very strong signal, given the extraordinary pressure they are under from the Russian attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure.”
He said “the most fundamental thing we can do in Europe now is to recommit to opening all clusters in respect of Ukraine’s application.” “That would send a powerful signal to the people of Ukraine that Europe is really progressing its pathway to accession,” he said.
The recent attacks are “appalling and horrific, and it illustrates that Putin is not interested in peace.”
“That’s why we must manifest our support for Ukraine in the practical ways … and certainly the membership agenda is one of those.”
'We very much regret this agreement on diesel,' Sweden's Kristersson says
Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson also offered his backing for Ukraine, as he criticised Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia.
“We very much regret this agreement on diesel. It’s obviously not a very big part, but still, it’s in the wrong direction. And every step now to help the Russians to increase their the financing of the war is a bad sign.
So we very much stick to Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s view on this.”
This 'senseless war of aggression' only continues because of Putin, Dutch PM says
EU leaders are now arriving for the European Council summit in Brussels and understandably they get asked about the latest situation in Ukraine.
Dutch PM Rob Jetten offered his strong backing for Ukraine and president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying “there is only one reason why this senseless war of aggression is continuing, and that’s because Putin chooses to do so.”
“He is the one that can end this war by starting negotiations for just and lasting peace. And as long as he doesn’t, the Ukrainians will have to defend themselves and defend European values, and we stand shoulder to shoulder with the Ukrainians.”
He urged other leaders “to do more financially, militarily, and non-militarily, because a lot of European countries are lagging behind in the support for Ukraine.”
“So let’s step up our game and make sure that they can win this senseless war.”
Starlink satellite restrictions highlight Europe's dependency on US technology
As Ukraine reported problems with Starlink satellite internet terminals and US data that warns of Russian ballistic missile attacks, Kyiv also faced the harsh reality that its European allies cannot offer any ready-made alternatives, Reuters reported.
European countries have voiced strong support for Ukraine and Zelenskyy. But the problems with vital data highlighted that Ukraine and Europe depend heavily on US systems for both low-orbit satellite communications – provided by SpaceX via Starlink – and space-based infrared sensing that feeds into early-warning systems.
A US satellite constellation called the Space-Based Infrared System provides early missile warnings.
As for Starlink, Europe does not have a ready-made alternative that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat soared on Wednesday following news of Ukraine’s difficulties with Starshield, fuelled by investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
Morning opening: Musk suggests US government was behind Starlink restrictions
Billionaire tech mogul Elon Musk has suggested that the US government could be behind the decision to restrict the speed of SpaceX’s satellite-technology used by Ukraine’s military.
In a post of X, he appeared to suggest the Trump administration was behind the move, which Ukraine says restricts its ability to use key defensive weapons.
Musk said:
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
In further posts overnight, reacting to Zelenskyy’s comments on his relationship with Donald Trump, Musk went further and appeared to suggest Zelenskyy should leave the post, saying it’s “time to go.”
In a TV interview with Piers Morgan, Zelenskyy said he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s decisions and worried about “losing a strong partner,” playing a critical role across Ukraine’s defence.
For what it’s worth, Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.
The issue is likely to come up again today and tomorrow as EU leaders meet in Brussels for key political talks on the future.
With today’s discussions focused on the bloc’s internal matters, including the EU’s next budget, Ukraine is expected to come up on Friday when Zelenskyy joins other leaders in Brussels. But the ongoing crisis in Ukraine’s relations with the US risks overshadowing the entire meeting.
I will bring you all the updates throughout the day.
It’s Thursday, 15 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

theguardian.com.title: Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business
theguardian.com.text:
Serbia’s authoritarian ruler personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower, the Guardian can reveal.
Aleksandar Vučić summoned officials to a meeting at his presidential offices about the project, which has culminated in a landmark indictment of senior figures from his regime on charges of abuse of public office.
The criminal case is believed to be the first resulting from the Trumps’ global moneymaking campaign, described by critics as a “pay to play” arrangement where everything from sanctions relief to cutting-edge chips is available to those who enrich the first family and their associates.
The alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October, when Vučić will seek to extend his 12 years in power in the face of a mass protest movement spurred by government corruption.
A nationalist former propaganda chief under Slobodan Milošević, Vučić hosted the US president’s son Donald Trump Jr and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Belgrade as they developed plans for a $500m hotel and residential tower to add to their global property portfolios.
After the abuse of power charges were brought last December, Kushner’s company announced the project would not proceed “at this time”. Vučić threatened reprisals, calling the prosecutors “corrupt gangs” who “fabricated cases”.
“We have lost an exceptional investment,” the Serbian president said. “I will personally ensure that everyone who participated in causing this damage is held accountable.”
Vučić’s culture minister is among those charged with abuse of power. But a Guardian investigation, drawing on interviews and leaked documents, reveals that the Serbian president himself led the initial meeting where the alleged scheme was discussed. This crucial meeting is not mentioned in the indictment, raising questions about what information the prosecutors are holding back and why.
Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner said they had no part in the removal of the building’s protected status and that it would be “false” to say the Belgrade project was part of a “pay to play” scheme.
Vučić did not respond to requests for comment. His decision to call a snap election means that a hearing at which witnesses might reveal details of his involvement will not take place until after the vote.
A free 99-year lease
On 6 February 2024, Dubravka Ğukanović, a Serbian conservation professor in her 60s, arrived for a meeting at the presidency, a domed former royal palace. For three years, she had been the director of the country’s institute for the protection of cultural monuments.
The topic was the General Staff building, the former Yugoslav ministry of defence in central Belgrade. The building, an architectural gem seen as an emblem of resistance to the Nazis, was already cherished when Nato forces bombed it in 1999 during its campaign to force Milošević to withdraw from Kosovo, deepening its resonance.
Vučić himself had reaffirmed the General Staff building’s legally protected status in 2016. Now, the president said he wanted Ğukanović to rescind it, according to two people with knowledge of the meeting. Some unspecified “foreign investor” was keen on the site.
Under Serbian law, stripping the General Staff building of its protected status was not in Ğukanović’s gift. Her institute would have to commission an expert opinion, which would have to conclude that there were good reasons why protected status was no longer merited.
But the president wanted it done. At 6ft 6in and intolerant of dissent, Vučić can be intimidating. His tone towards Ğukanović and another heritage official present was unpleasant, the sources said. He told them they were lazy and incompetent. The message was clear: do what I want or resign.
A plausible explanation for Vučić’s forceful intervention came the following month, when an agreement between the Serbian government and Kushner’s real estate company leaked.
Married to Trump’s daughter Ivanka, Kushner had been an influential White House aide during his father-in-law’s first term. Since Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election, Kushner had been concentrating on his investment fund.
By early 2024, Trump was storming to the Republican nomination and was favourite to win the coming election. If Trump took back the White House, Kushner would once more be one of the most influential people on the planet.
The leaked agreement showed the Serbian authorities had granted Kushner’s company a 99-year lease over the General Staff site, free of charge.
Kushner, whose spokesperson said he had been looking at the project since 2021, posted an image of the design on X, professing himself “excited”.
The news was not universally welcomed in Belgrade. “Serbia is not a buffet, and Vučić is not a waiter,” said Aleksandar Jovanović Ćuta, an environmental activist who revealed the agreement. “This is not his private property.”
Yet Vučić’s regime proceeded to sign a contract, dated 13 May 2024 and seen by the Guardian, undertaking that the “cultural heritage designation” of the site would be removed “to the satisfaction” of Kushner’s company.
Comply or resign
The week after the contract was signed, Ğukanović was summoned to another meeting. The president was not there this time. Siniša Mali, his finance minister and right-hand man, took charge.
Mali urged Ğukanović and Olivera Vučković, Belgrade’s top heritage official, to cancel the General Staff site’s protected status, according to the indictment’s summary of testimony the two women would later give prosecutors. It makes no reference to the earlier meeting with the president but indicates that the subject had previously been broached.
“Mali asked them if they had given it any thought,” the indictment says, “and if they would initiate the procedure to remove the building’s protected status.”
The women refused, “believing that the legal conditions for it were not met”. In that case, Mali told them, repeating his boss’s ultimatum from February, they should resign. They did.
In her resignation letter, which the Guardian has seen, Ğukanović wrote that she could not agree “to inappropriate interventions that would permanently destroy all the values of the complex, which testifies to the highest achievements of contemporary Serbian architecture and is of incalculable importance for preserving enduring creative values, the education of future generations, and the strengthening of the cultural identity of the Serbian people”.
Approached by the Guardian, Ğukanović and Vučković confirmed the accuracy of this account. Ğukanović added: “I prefer not to make any statement on this matter while the court proceedings are ongoing.”
Little was heard of the General Staff plan for months. In November, Trump beat Kamala Harris to win re-election. Ten days later, Vučić’s government announced that the General Staff site had been stripped of its protected status.
Keeping it in the family
One of the first things Trump did upon regaining the presidency was to ditch the pledge he made in his first term that his family business would refrain from doing deals abroad while he was in office.
“The scale of corruption will be orders of magnitude greater than what we saw in the first Trump administration,” Kathleen Clark, a government ethics lawyer at Washington University School of Law, warned at the time. Trump had made it much easier, she said, to buy his favour.
The family business remained officially under the control of his two oldest sons, Don Jr and Eric. In January 2025, four days after their father’s inauguration, Eric spoke about some new projects. The Trumps and the Kushners, New York real estate families united by marriage, had decided to embark on their first venture together: Kushner’s Belgrade hotel and tower would bear the Trump name.
“It’s going to be fun to bring the family together,” Eric told the New York Times. “Serbia is one of the fastest-growing countries in Europe, and we’re incredibly honoured to be there.” Kushner, who had travelled to Belgrade for what Vučić called an “inspiring” meeting with the Serbian leader, added: “Our research showed that the Trump brand would be the best for this market.”
That brand has enjoyed a surge in demand around the world during Trump’s second term, accompanied by allegations that it comes with a quid pro quo.
In Vietnam, Eric was showered with confetti at the groundbreaking ceremony for a £1.5bn golf resort, the permits for which were granted with unusual speed. Then Trump halved Vietnam’s tariffs. The Saudis poured money into Kushner’s fund, and plans emerged for a Trump plaza in Jeddah. Then Trump agreed to sell the kingdom new US fighter jets. A cryptocurrency baron’s company and senior Emiratis cut a lucrative transaction with World Liberty Financial, the digital currency venture Don Jr and Eric founded. Trump gave the crypto baron a pardon and the Emiratis access to restricted US chips.
Asked about such deals last year, Kushner, now a presidential envoy to Russia, Israel and elsewhere, said: “What people call conflicts of interests … I call experience and trusted relationships that we have throughout the world.”
Those who strike up “trusted relationships” with the Trumps, even if there is not an obvious quid pro quo, gain something less tangible but maybe still more valuable: the aura of friendship with a president who is happy to wield his superpower to make or break smaller nations and their leaders.
Vučić has plenty in common with Trump. Both are friendly with Vladimir Putin and contemptuous of the EU – in Vučić’s case, despite his country having applied to join. A shared disdain for Nato may help explain why the one part of the General Staff building’s heritage that the redevelopment pledged to retain was a memorial to the alliance’s “aggression” against Serbia.
And there is a lot that Vučić could use US help with, not least the fate of Kosovo, which he says is still part of Serbia.
Not long after his father returned to office, Don Jr landed in Belgrade. Vučić said that during their meeting he “emphasised the importance of the economic and political relations between Serbia and the USA and stressed the importance of strategic cooperation between the two countries and joint projects in the years to come”. When Don Jr returned the following month, Vučić fed him a choice sucking-pig.
For Vučić, the support of the first family was timely. Days before his regime stripped the General Staff site of its protection, the collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people, triggered rolling protests against graft. The student organisers’ slogan has become “Serbia or mafia”.
Don Jr’s visit came on the eve of the biggest demonstration in Serbia’s history. He invited Vučić on to his podcast, Triggered, and declared that the Serb ruler’s opponents were “weaponising” the Novi Sad disaster, just as Trump’s had done with the Capitol riots after his 2020 election defeat.
But the protesters maintained their momentum, and began to rally against the Trump tower. In May 2025, Vučić went to the US, hoping to visit Trump at Mar-a-Lago, his Florida members’ club. He got to see Rudy Giuliani, Trump’s disgraced lawyer, but not the president. State media reported this was because Vučić fell ill.
No sooner was Vučić home than police arrested Goran Vasić, the man who had been installed as head of the heritage institute to replace Dubravka Ğukanović following her resignation. To achieve the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protected status, prosecutors said, Vasic had forged a supportive expert opinion.
More arrests followed. In December 2025, Vučić’s culture minister was indicted for abuse of office for his alleged part in the General Staff scheme. Within days, Kushner’s company announced the project was off.
Coup or cover-up?
Vučić’s threat of reprisals was not idle.
His allies attacked Ğukanović, claiming that she had tried to profit personally from her time as a heritage official. Her deputy, who received a visit from the state security service after she went on television to denounce the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protection, has been accused of unrelated misconduct. The Serbian conservators’ industry body said this had “the obvious aim of discrediting her”. Both are expected to give evidence in the criminal proceedings.
For the specialist unit of organised-crime prosecutors who brought the charges, this is a watershed case. Never before has a serving Serbian minister been indicted.
Vučić accuses the prosecutors of staging a coup. Others, though, fear they are pulling their punches. That concern increased when Nikola Selaković, the indicted culture minister, used a court appearance in April to reveal that, while police were raiding his ministry, he was in his office sipping plum brandy and smoking cigarettes with Mladen Nenadić, the head of the organised-crime prosecutors’ unit. The unit’s spokesperson said there was “no discussion regarding the course of the case”.
“In everything that happened regarding potential investments, I saw a chance for our country and citizens,” said Selaković, who faces three years in prison if convicted.
Vučić has not been charged. Neither has his lieutenant, Mali. Both deny wrongdoing.
The indictment refers to evidence from witnesses who were present at the Vučić meeting in February 2024 but does not mention it, raising questions about the apparent decision to omit what would appear to be a key part of the narrative.
The spokesperson for the organised crime prosecutors’ unit said that it had evidence regarding Vučić’s February 2024 meeting with the heritage officials. Beyond those already indicted, prosecutors were “conducting pretrial proceedings in this case to determine potential criminal liability of other persons as well”, the spokesperson added.
Vučić has stepped down and cannot seek another term but is expected to retain his control over the regime if he is elected prime minister on 25 October. In one of his last acts as president, he issued 49 pardons. Some of the recipients have not been identified and it is not clear whether they include defendants in the General Staff case.
The White House referred questions to the Trumps’ company. Its representative said: “The Trump Organization has no plans to develop any project in Belgrade, was never, at any point, involved in any discussions or negotiations to acquire any site in Belgrade and denies any involvement in or knowledge of the alleged claims.”
Kushner’s spokesperson said: “The suggestion that Jared Kushner pursued the Belgrade project as part of any political arrangement or ‘pay to play’ scheme is categorically false.” Rather, it was “an opportunity to transform a site associated with a painful chapter in Serbia’s history into a symbol of healing and reconciliation, while bringing substantial private investment, jobs and economic opportunity to Belgrade”.
The spokesperson added: “Jared had no involvement in the Serbian government’s internal processes concerning the site’s protected status.”
For all Vučić’s difficulties, the tale of the Trump Tower Belgrade does not appear to have put others off doing business with the first family. Trump retains stakes in dozens of his companies, even if his sons nominally run them. In July, he released his financial disclosure for his first year back at the White House. It showed he had made $2bn.

theguardian.com.title: Man killed by tiger at Yorkshire zoo had bouts of psychosis, inquest hears
theguardian.com.text:
A man who was killed by a tiger at a South Yorkshire zoo had bouts of psychosis, his family told an inquest opening, as they expressed concerns about his contact with mental health services before his death.
William Chapman was mauled to death by the animal at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster on Saturday, after climbing into its enclosure.
The 24-year-old had been diagnosed with schizophrenia but was “highly functioning and independent with no care requirements”, the hearing at Doncaster coroner’s court heard.
He was under the care of local mental health services, but the coroner’s officer Caitlin Brookes said his family had expressed “a number of concerns” in relation to his contact with them. Brookes said the Rotherham, Doncaster and South Humber NHS foundation trust had launched an investigation after Chapman’s death.
The inquest heard Chapman was a self-employed online trader who was living in Doncaster at the time of his death. An initial postmortem examination found that he had died from multiple traumatic injuries after his encounter with the tiger.
The inquest heard he attended Yorkshire Wildlife Park on 10 October, and, at about 1.30pm, climbed over two fences and entered the enclosure housing the 200kg male Siberian tiger named Altai.
Brookes said: “He was approached by the tiger and the ensuing physical contact between the tiger and Mr Chapman led to him sustaining multiple traumatic injuries which rapidly led to his death.”
Park staff secured the tiger, and paramedics attended but confirmed Chapman’s death at the scene. The senior coroner, Nicola Mundy, said her office was awaiting a more substantial report on the extent of Chapman’s injuries.
The inquest heard Chapman’s stepfather had travelled to the mortuary to identify him on 13 October. The inquest heard his full name was William Harry Bruce Chapman and that he was born in 2002 in Chichester.
Mundy said Chapman’s family “were finding things incredibly difficult” and had decided not to attend the hearing, but would be updated afterwards by her staff.
His family spoke out on Wednesday after the US president, Donald Trump, shared a video of the attack with his 13 million followers on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday. Trump followed this with an AI-generated video of himself play-fighting with the tiger, which ends with him and the tiger hugging.
Chapman’s family said online footage being shared was “deeply offensive” and causing them “severe distress”.
They also shared a tribute to him, writing: “William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved – and William loved them back. Sadly, William suffered from significant mental illness over a number of years and was consequently prescribed strong medication.”
As a child, Chapman appeared in ITV’s 2009 comedy drama May Contain Nuts and in BBC Learning’s True Stories series, according to IMDb. He previously attended Jackie Palmer stage school in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, which paid tribute on Facebook and posted a picture of Chapman as a child student.
City of Doncaster council, which is responsible for licensing the park, is carrying out a health and safety investigation and said it would share the outcome with the coroner, the hearing was told.
Wildlife and zoo experts previously told the Guardian it was unlikely Yorkshire Wildlife Park could have done anything to prevent the death. The park said staff were receiving specialist support and that Altai, a member of an endangered species, would not be euthanised.
A full inquest will be held on 18 March next year.

theguardian.com.title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt
theguardian.com.text:
An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.
Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5%, respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.
Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in the memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI.
The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst performance since July.
The sell-off came after US data showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher-than-expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.
The figure has rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.
“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said.
Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”
The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets was putting world financial stability at risk.
“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the IMF said. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.
The latest jitters hit China, where the Shanghai Shenzhen CSI 300 slipped by as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.
European stocks were skewing lower at the start of trading, with the Europe Stoxx 600 down by 0.4%, the UK’s FTSE 100 down 0.06%, France’s CAC 40 down 0.19%, and Spain’s Ibex falling 0.17%. Germany’s DAX fell by 0.53%.
In the US, stock futures pointed to losses for tech stocks, with the Nasdaq 100 futures dropping 1%.

theguardian.com.title: Albania’s prime minister vows not to resign over student-led protests
theguardian.com.text:
Albania’s prime minister, Edi Rama, has said he will not resign over student-led demonstrations, as protesters and police clashed in the country’s capital for a third consecutive day.
Police used teargas and water cannon to disperse demonstrators marching along several main roads around Tirana, while protests spread to other cities.
Demonstrators are demanding Rama’s resignation and more support for students in the country, citing poor university conditions and high tuition fees.
“As for calls for my resignation, governments are changed through democratic elections. We had elections last year, not a revolution,” Rama said in written responses to Reuters.
“My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward. The alternative would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership.”
Rama said he would be ready to discuss the rising cost of education, but added: “Attacking institutions, destroying public property and threatening public safety have nothing to do with the legitimate demands of students.”
There were hours of violent clashes between police and demonstrators in Tirana on Tuesday and Wednesday, when protesters smashed their way into several government buildings and set at least one on fire.
Police said 51 officers were injured during Wednesday’s protests and 65 people were arrested on suspicion of “attacking police officers, institutions, public and private property”.
Police did not give figures for the number of protesters hurt but Tirana public hospital reported that “seven protesters injured in the violence sought medical treatment”.
The protests mark the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who won a fourth term last year.
The unrest follows months of mostly peaceful demonstrations sparked by plans to build a luxury resort on Albania’s southern coast backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, a project that has faced legal challenges.
“Corruption must be confronted and, as the EU itself has recently reaffirmed, Albania is tackling it as never before,” Rama said.
“Perhaps some forces, at home and abroad, do not want Albania to succeed as a forerunner for EU membership. But I will not allow violence to derail Albania’s European future.”
The EU’s delegation in Tirana repeated its earlier calls for de-escalation, strongly condemning the “violent escalation at the protest and the destruction of public and private property”.
“We call on protesters to exercise restraint and to refrain from any acts of violence. Violence has no place in democracies,” it said in a statement.
Along with Montenegro, Albania is leading the EU accession process among Balkan countries and is aiming for entry as early as 2028.

theguardian.com.title: Russia and Ukraine resume energy strikes despite Trump warnings
theguardian.com.text:
The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to.
Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it was the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, after briefly halting them to demonstrate that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked the gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.
Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire, the ministry claimed.
In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three and injured six.
“The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement.
Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 850 Shahed drones at a time when the speed of Ukraine’s defensive capabilities was being “artificially restricted”, a reference to the sudden limitations on Ukraine’s use of the Starlink and Starshield mobile internet terminals.
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in his social media post on X, referring to a growing quarrel with the Trump administration. “Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies. We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security.”
Trump suddenly declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, writing on TruthSocial: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”
Despite Trump’s claims, however, Russia continued to launch heavy strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, using hypersonic and ballistic missiles to target key Ukrainian power plants, leaving cities including Kyiv without power and water for hours. Ukraine said it would not strike Russian oil refineries in the interim in order to show that it was ready for negotiations.
But the White House piled pressure on Zelenskyy to capitulate to Russia by threatening to cut programmes to deliver arms to Ukraine and to stop sharing US battlefield intelligence with Ukraine.
The US appeared to make good on some threats. Ukraine said it had not received advance warning from Washington of Russian missile strikes for several days this week. And on Wednesday, Ukrainian soldiers also complained that their access to Starshield programmes controlled by the US military had been restricted, scuppering drone missions on the frontlines.
The feud between Zelenskyy and Trump has spun out of control over the last week. Trump, who believes that his support for Ukraine should come with a degree of control over the country’s leadership, has said that Ukraine should “get a new president”.
Asked on Thursday by Piers Morgan whether he felt betrayed, Zelenskyy said yes. “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner,” he said.
Musk, the powerful head of SpaceX, which produces the Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military, has emerged as a top critic of Zelenskyy in the US.
On Thursday, Musk denied throttling the Starlink systems and said they were controlled by the US government. But in a social media post commenting on a Zelenskyy statement that Ukraine would continue to fight until Russia’s defeat, he wrote: “And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go.”

theguardian.com.title: US officials considering ad campaign to urge South African Afrikaners to emigrate
theguardian.com.text:
The US government could spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on a media campaign in South Africa to figure out why more white Afrikaners are not applying to become refugees to the US, as Donald Trump had hoped.
State department officials, according to an August proposal seen by the Guardian, outlined a roughly $335,000 research and advertising effort after applications to the refugee program “trended lower than expected” since Afrikaners were allowed to apply directly online in November 2025. The document, written by the US mission in South Africa with a department research unit for the embassy in Pretoria, admits officials know little about why.
“There’s currently little research about why Afrikaners are not applying to request referral into the US Refugee Admissions Program,” the proposal reads.
The focus on Afrikaners flows from a February 2025 executive order directing officials to put Afrikaner resettlement first while the broader refugee program stayed suspended. Administration officials had said Afrikaners face racial discrimination and “white genocide”. The South African government has rejected the genocide claims, and experts have widely dismissed the idea that Afrikaners face targeted violence or genocide.
Last year, the president restricted refugee admissions to 7,500, the lowest in US history, then raised it to 17,500 in May, with the added slots again going primarily to Afrikaners. The overall cap was 125,000 under Joe Biden.
The US admitted 16,292 refugees in the fiscal year that ended 30 September, according to its most recent data reporting. The remaining five were Afghans: three from last November and two from September. A year earlier, South Africans made up 342 of 38,102 refugee admissions.
The state department plan would proceed in three phases. The pitch suggests focus groups would be held in Pretoria and Krugersdorp in Gauteng, Bloemfontein and Kroonstad in Free State, Stellenbosch and Worcester in Western Cape and Kimberley and Orania in the Northern Cape, with the latter being an Afrikaner-only separatist community. Every location would host two age groups, 20 to 35 and 40 to 55, with participants grouped by urban or rural setting and household income. A survey of 1,000 Afrikaners, online and offline, would then test which messages work in which communities.
The final phase is a six-month digital campaign, mostly in Afrikaans with possibly some English, aimed at Afrikaners “interested in migrating”. Because the community is hard to reach through conventional social and press channels, the proposal says, the department would hire an agency with local knowledge and use “trusted messengers”.
In response, a spokesperson with the state department said “we continue to process and admit as refugees Afrikaners in South Africa who are escaping the threat of government-sponsored race-based discrimination”.
“President Trump has been very clear that we are prioritizing the resettlement of Afrikaners in South Africa who are escaping government-sponsored race-based discrimination,” as part of US policy from the executive order, the spokesperson added.
Trump’s 2025 order alleged “South Africa has taken aggressive positions towards the United States and its allies, including accusing Israel, not Hamas, of genocide in the International Court of Justice, and reinvigorating its relations with Iran to develop commercial, military, and nuclear arrangements.”
This year’s Nobel peace prize went to Navi Pillay, the South African judge who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza, causing Trump to rave on Truth Social: “I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else!” and that the prize should have gone to “the Great United States of America, whose Representative, ME, settled eight Wars, and many other things”.
The South African government, for its part, has rejected the claim of genocide as unfounded and politically motivated. In New York last month, foreign minister Ronald Lamola said “there is no evidence” for the genocide claim. Pretoria has also argued that few South Africans have taken up the offer, which it says shows the claims are false.
The refugee program is one piece in a broader rupture. Trump announced last November that South Africa would not be invited to the 2026 G20 summit, which the US is hosting in Miami in mid-December, citing alleged abuses against white farmers. Washington has also cut aid and restricted visas over South Africa’s race and land policies.
Last month, the US ambassador in Pretoria, Leo Brent Bozell III, wrote in an op-ed that his government was “shocked” by what it saw as Pretoria’s silence on a set of US requests. He cited concern over the country’s 2024 Expropriation Act and a push to make rural crime a priority.
The administration is also putting money behind the cause. Just before funds expired, it moved to direct more than $175m from the state department’s Human Rights and Democracy Fund to 43 grants worth $176.9m, as the Guardian has reported. That is most of the $205m Congress appropriated for the fund, which bolsters rightwing causes abroad.
One is a $1m grant meant for “advancing white Afrikaner rights” in South Africa and for collecting data on abuses against minorities. No recipient has been named. Sources with knowledge of the awards process told the Guardian that administration figures lobbied personally for the awards, reflecting the priorities of JD Vance on European cultural identity and Stephen Miller on immigration and support for white minorities.
The bureau that runs refugee admissions has new leadership. Adam Zerbinopoulos, a career diplomat, became its senior official on 31 August.

theguardian.com.title: Key US voters say economy is getting worse ahead of midterms, exclusive poll finds
theguardian.com.text:
With the midterm elections less than three weeks away, key voting groups including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans are increasingly disenchanted with Donald Trump’s economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.
The majority of those surveyed were pessimistic about the economy, with three quarters of Americans saying they are concerned about a recession while 61% wrongly believe that the US is already experiencing one. By its typical definition, the US is not currently experiencing a recession.
The poll shows growing weariness across the political spectrum over high prices.
Republicans, fighting to keep control of Congress, are losing support with independent voters, who are expected to be the deciding factor in key swing races. Nearly two-thirds (65%) of independents said the economy is worse, up from 48% who said the same in September 2024 in the heat of the 2024 presidential election.
Even within the Republican ranks, optimism has waned. In February 2025, just a few weeks after Trump was inaugurated, 39% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By February 2026, just before the US launched attacks against Iran, that optimism was up to 49%. In the latest poll, just 28% of Republicans said the economy is getting better.
Voters say the high prices they are seeing at gas stations and grocery stores will be a key factor when they cast their votes in November. Two-thirds of those polled said that gas prices and grocery prices are their most important issues heading into the election, followed by living expenses, healthcare costs and foreign affairs.
Recent inflation data showed that annualized prices increased 3.7% in September, the highest reading before a midterm election, excluding the pandemic, since 1990.
Energy prices have been especially high since the Iran war, with average gas prices at the pump crossing $1.20 more per gallon compared with a year ago. California drivers, who are experiencing the highest gas prices, are paying on average $6.20 per gallon, according to AAA.
Democrats in swing races have spent much of the last few months framing their midterm battles as a fight, in part, against a growing affordability crisis. James Talarico, the Democratic candidate in a closely watched US Senate race in Texas, has a campaign ad of him holding a paper bag of groceries. “Too many Texans feel like they’re drowning, the cost of groceries, gas, healthcare,” he says in the video.
“They say I can’t win because of my name,” Abdul el-Sayed, another Democratic candidate for a US Senate race in Michigan, said at a recent campaign event. “My name is not the reason your gas prices are through the roof. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”
In the new poll, a vast majority of Americans agreed that there is an affordability crisis, including 96% of Republicans. But Americans still remain divided over who has a solution.
- Democrats (71%) were more likely than Republicans (59%) to say that their own party had a solution.
- Republicans were more likely (26%) to say neither party has a solution compared with Democrats (17%)
- Half of independents said neither party has a solution, while 14% sided with Democrats and 10% with Republicans.
Rural Americans, considered a core base for Trump, were more likely to believe that neither party has a solution (41%) compared to their suburban (35%) and urban (27%) counterparts. Four out of 10 of rural Americans said they are living in “survival mode”, where one surprise bill could sink them, compared with 35% of urban and 27% of suburban Americans.
When asked what is most affecting today’s gas prices, 46% of rural Americans said the US government compared with 28% of Republicans who said the same. Republicans were the least likely of any group to blame the US government, instead spreading the blame across oil companies, the Iranian government and natural economic fluctuations.
This survey was conducted online within the US by The Harris Poll from 24 September to 3 October 2026 among a nationally representative sample of 3,998 US adults.

theguardian.com.title: UK threatens to ban Eritreans over returns policy
theguardian.com.text:
Eritreans could be stopped from coming to the UK unless the country agrees to accept more rejected asylum seekers and criminals, Shabana Mahmood has warned.
VIPs and officials from the east African country have already been stripped of fast-track access to UK visas after their government refused to cooperate with the return of its nationals, the home secretary said.
The warning comes after Eritrea abruptly withdrew returns cooperation earlier this year, the Home Office said.
Refugee organisations have warned that the UK should not get drawn into rejecting applicants for asylum from Eritrea because it is a war-torn country and the UK usually accepts the vast majority of applicants, who are often escaping famine and conflict.
Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat in the year ending June 2026. Returns arrangements are vital for removing people who have been refused asylum and foreign criminals.
Mahmood said: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused.
“My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK.
“I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.”
The move follows similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2025.
Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to cooperate with demands on migrant returns, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo faced visa restrictions before reaching an agreement with the UK in February.
In March, ministers also placed an emergency brake on visas for nationals from four countries after the home secretary accused them of exploiting Britain’s generosity to claim asylum.
Study visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan were also halted, as were work visas for Afghans.
Just over 100 refused asylum seekers from Eritrea have been deported – a figure comprising less than 4% of the 2,626 people whose claims were rejected in the past four years. Nearly 6,000 Eritreans have reached the UK across the Channel in the year to June, the highest number of any nationality.
After the success of the previous sanction threats, Mahmood warned other countries that they faced similar visa restrictions if they continued to refuse to take back their criminals, illegal migrants and rejected asylum seekers.
India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Somalia, Egypt and Gabon have been identified as resistant to taking back illegal migrants and could face sanctions.
Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said roughly 7,000 applications for asylum came from Eritreans, about 8% of the total.
About 84% are successful on first application and more will be successful on appeal, she said.
“There are different types of threats that can be made such as stopping student visas, or stopping visit visas. It will be interesting to see what kind of impact this has on the number of returns.”
Reacting to Mahmood’s announcement, one Eritrean asylum seeker said any returnees would “be put in prison and may never be able to get out”.
The advocacy group Justice for Eritreans condemned the announcement. “Many Eritreans have fled indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and severe human rights abuses,” it said. “These risks cannot be ignored for the sake of immigration targets. Refugee protection is a legal responsibility, not a political bargaining tool.”
UN experts say that the human rights situation in Eritrea continues to be dire. Mohamed Abdelsalam Babiker, the special rapporteur on human rights in Eritrea, said there were no signs of meaningful improvement in the country’s human rights situation.
“There remain reasonable grounds to believe that crimes against humanity continue in Eritrea,” he said when launching a report this year into the human rights situation.
“Regrettably, the core human rights issues that prompted the creation of this mandate 14 years ago remain mostly unresolved.
“The ongoing systematic, and widespread enforced disappearance and prolonged incommunicado detention without charge or trial, torture, and the persecution of political opponents, journalists, and members of religious communities remain central features of governance in Eritrea.”
Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International’s policy lead on refugee and migrant rights, said: “As Amnesty and others have documented, Eritrea has an appalling human rights record.
“It has not become any less unsafe following the election in this country of a Labour government in 2024 or Shabana Mahmood beginning her term at the Home Office in 2025.”
Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “Severe political repression and widespread human rights abuses are the reason people are forced to flee Eritrea, and are, in the vast majority of cases, recognised by our government as in need of support.
“It’s imperative that this policy only targets the Eritrean authorities, and does not undermine the UK’s moral and legal duty to provide protection to those who need it.”

theguardian.com.title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
theguardian.com.text:
Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.
More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.
The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.
The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.
Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”
Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority.
Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises.
The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.
While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.
Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.
“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”
She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.
The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence.
LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country.
The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination.
The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-Saharan Africa towards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people.
There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso within the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.
In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislation criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislation first proposed in 2021. In 2023, Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act made homosexual acts punishable by death.

theguardian.com.title: Woman charged after allegedly poisoning colleague’s curry lunch with snail pellets
theguardian.com.text:
A woman has been charged after allegedly poisoning a co-worker’s lunch curry with snail pellets.
Western Australian police say a 58-year-old woman brought a container of curry to share with colleagues at her workplace in Perth’s southern suburbs in February.
A 43-year-old woman allegedly contaminated it with snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance, a police spokesperson said on Thursday.
“The curry had been shared among employees and consumed without issue during a morning tea break,” police said.
“After the meal, the accused accessed a chemical storage shed and later entered the staff lunch room where the food was kept.”
At lunchtime, the alleged victim went to eat some more of her curry.
When she opened the container, she spotted bright green granules in the food.
“After tasting a small amount, (she) experienced numbness to her tongue,” the police spokesperson said.
It will be alleged the accused and the victim were in a personal relationship.
Detectives arrested the 43-year-old woman last week.
She has been charged with one count of unlawful act or omission with intent to harm (endangering the life, health or safety of any person).
She is scheduled to appear before Armadale magistrates court on 5 November.
Police declined to provide further information about the relationship or the workplace.

theguardian.com.title: ADF member ‘person of interest’ after video recorder found in HMAS Leeuwin women’s showers
theguardian.com.text:
The defence department says a member of the Australian Defence Force is a “person of interest” in investigations after a video recording device was found in a bathroom on HMAS Leeuwin, in what the chief of navy called a “despicable betrayal of trust”.
A day after senator Jacqui Lambie told the Senate that a hidden camera had been found in a female shower facility onboard the naval ship, docked in Cairns, navy chief Matt Buckley confirmed a “video recording device” had been located in one of the ship’s bathrooms.
In a statement, Vice Adm Buckley called the incident an “act of sexual violence” and “the most despicable betrayal of trust”, and said the navy was conducting a review of all bathrooms across the service.
Defence confirmed on Wednesday that a “video recording device” was found in the cabin of the vessel, which it had referred to the Joint Military Police Unit. It came hours after Lambie – an ADF veteran and advocate for defence personnel – told the Senate she’d been contacted by a former member of the navy with allegations about a camera being found aboard HMAS Leeuwin.
Defence did not initially confirm where the device had been found, or any details about its investigation.
On Thursday, the department gave a further update.
“An Australian Defence Force member has been identified as a person of interest in the investigation into a video recording device being located on Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin,” the department said.
“This person is now assisting the Joint Military Police Unit with its enquiries. Navy’s focus and priority is providing support to those who are impacted by this incident.”
In a written statement, Buckley informed navy members of the update.
“I consider this a most serious matter, and accordingly, the Ship’s program has been altered to enable a rapid and rigorous investigation by the Joint Military Policing Unit,” he wrote.
“My highest priority, as always, is the wellbeing of our people.”
Buckley said the navy was conducting a “100% audit of all of our bathrooms across the Fleet”.
“This act is the most despicable betrayal of trust and is fundamentally misaligned with our values,” he said.
“You have my assurance and commitment that we will tackle this act of sexual violence with all of our energy. Any perpetrator will be held to account. Further, you should all know that eradicating sexual violence in our workplace is fundamental to the fighting efficiency of our Navy. I invite all of you to make this your priority.”
The defence minister, Richard Marles, described the incident as “reprehensible, invasive and … the most despicable breach of trust”. He said he was receiving updates on the investigation as it continued.
“There is no place for this behaviour in the Australian Defence Force. Our priority remains supporting the individuals who have been impacted,” he said in a statement on social media on Thursday.
On Wednesday, Lambie asked whether images captured by the device had been published online.
Buckley said “all potentially impacted personnel are receiving our strongest support”, adding that the warrant officer of the navy was in Cairns to support the ship’s company.

Pocock says interest rate rises should be replaced as companies ‘making bank’

The independent senator has told the ABC there were “a bunch” of alternatives to interest rates. He said:
We could start with something like a windfall profits tax. We’re seeing companies make absolute bank off the war in Iran, and most of those profits are flowing overseas. We’ve got this blunt instrument [of interest rates] and it clearly just is not working at the moment.
I don’t know why we keep just smashing Aussie households, raising unemployment, where clearly there are so many other factors at play.
You look at some of the big companies that paid zero tax, or, you know, 1.5% tax, while banking huge, huge revenue and profits. That’s got to end. That is also adding to inflation, but we’re not addressing it.

I kind of understand and agree with [what] the Greens said, that probably militarism is a curse on modern society. I wish we would have lived in a very peaceful time and country where our borders are intact, our sovereignty is protected by international law. Unfortunately, it’s not the case for us.

This person is now assisting the Joint Military Police Unit with its enquiries. Navy’s focus and priority is providing support to those who are impacted by this incident.
Hume says Coalition probably opposed to private health cuts even if pensioners exempt
The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, says Coalition members “don’t like” any effort to cut private health rebates for older Australians, as Labor looks for a deal.
Hume has told the ABC she “absolutely” supports the expansion of aged care beds that Labor has said the reforms would pay for.
But she indicated the Coalition would not be interested in negotiations for partial exemptions, such as for people on the full pension.
We don’t like the idea that older Australians are being targeted to have their health insurance, their private health insurance rebates removed from them …
Philosophically, we want more older Australians to have private health insurance, to take the pressure off the private health, the public sector, so that all Australians can benefit from our public health system. That is older Australians paying for themselves. Now there was an incentive to do that. It was a fair incentive, but the government wants to take that away.
Hume said the government could fund the aged care reforms from other areas, like winding back the National Reconstruction fund, the Housing Australia future fund and what she described as “climate bureaucracy”, including electric vehicle subsidies.
‘On what planet are you charging for a TV?’: Butler hits out at aged care providers
The health minister has skewered aged care providers for charging residents extra fees for basic services like TV.
Guardian Australia exposed the practice in July and recent ABC reporting has found new fee structure have made the problem worse.
Mark Butler has told the ABC he discussed the issue with providers earlier this week. He said:
I’ve been going to aged care facilities regularly since the early 1990s. TVs have been there for ever. Like, on what planet are you charging an extra service fee for a TV? It has been a basic entitlement for people in aged care facilities in their rooms as long as I can remember. …
I do not consider TVs extra services. I made that really clear to them … I’m not going to sort of do a rule-in rule-out, but TVs are pretty basic … I think that [wifi] is too.
